summary: Real-world 3D reconstruction pipelines often rely on multi-view images degraded by lossy compression. While compression artifacts have been extensively studied in single-image or video restoration, their impact on multi-view geometry remains largely overlooked. In this work, we identify compression-induced cross-view geometric inconsistency as a critical failure mode, where view-dependent artifacts disrupt feature matching, dense correspondence, camera parameter estimation, and downstream 3D reconstruction tasks such as novel view synthesis. To address this problem, we propose CompMVR, a compression-aware multi-view diffusion restoration framework that jointly refines compressed views while preserving cross-view consistency, and construct compressed datasets for systematic evaluation. Unlike conventional restoration methods that optimize each image independently for 2D perceptual quality, CompMVR leverages learned compression priors and cross-view correspondence to recover visual details while improving geometric reliability across views. Experiments across diverse datasets, codecs, and compression levels demonstrate gains in restoration quality and downstream 3D tasks, including novel-view synthesis, camera pose estimation, and view matching. These results establish compressed multi-view restoration as a distinct problem and highlight its importance for 3D reconstruction under lossy compression. Code and data for this paper are available at https://mchaewon.github.io/CompMVR-project-page/.
title: CompMVR: Compression-Aware Multi-View Restoration Using Diffusion Models for Geometrically Consistent 3D Reconstruction

summary: Supervised pairwise graph representations convert pairwise predictive relations into sample-specific graphs, but graph-level accuracy does not by itself show that higher-order topology carries the signal. In a controlled Transformer error-detection task, supervised pairwise graphs outperform attention-as-adjacency (ROC-AUC $0.839$ versus $0.559$; the comparable no-confidence pair is $0.687$ versus $0.559$), but their apparent advantage over model confidence disappears after controlling for sequence length, which is almost perfectly recoverable from the pooled hidden state ($R^2=0.9995$). On published HCP Emotion ensemble graphs, signed node aggregation already acts as an ensemble of supervised pairwise predictions. Edge magnitude alone is near chance; topology-aware augmentations change ROC-AUC by at most $0.004$, with only sign-separated degree showing small positive changes across all tested graph sizes, while a validation-tuned three-layer GCN provides no measurable improvement over the signed node-summary baseline. A Fisher post-hoc corrector satisfies its distribution-agnostic guarantees across the evaluated feature representations and remains stable under reduced labelled budgets; in a near-error-free fMRI calibration regime the bound correctly becomes statistically uninformative. A separate cross-attention analysis identifies a redundant reversal circuit and downstream EOS-timing and copy failures. Higher-order topology should therefore be credited only after local supervised evidence and recoverable nuisance variables have been excluded.
title: Interpreting Supervised Pairwise Graph Representations: Local Evidence, Confounding, and Provable Post-hoc Correction

summary: Websites and applications deploy CAPTCHAs and anti-automation mechanisms that use behavioral signals such as interaction trajectories and timing, not outcomes alone, to distinguish humans from automated agents. We call these protected GUI environments, where correctly solving a verification task is insufficient for end-to-end task completion. Agents must turn solver outputs into accepted interactions and adapt execution to runtime feedback under time constraints. We introduce SolveBind, a GUI-agent framework combining hierarchical solving with runtime supervision. A hierarchical solving tree decomposes verification into interdependent Perceive, Ground, Solve, Act, and Verify capabilities. A runtime supervisor grounds action commitments in tool-derived evidence, revises them as evidence arrives, and mediates execution under explicit recovery budgets. Across nine CAPTCHA task families and nine backbone models, SolveBind achieves the highest success rate on eight backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 13.3-34.5 percentage points. It achieves the highest success rate on all six AndroidWorld backbones. In a paired GPT-5.5 analysis, MobileAgent produces correct answers but fails dynamic verification on 13 of 90 tasks; SolveBind succeeds on seven of these tasks. With automatic submission, removing binding reduces success from 82.22% to 71.56% and increases latency and token usage. Recovery caps reduce execution cost with a small observed success trade-off: removing them raises success from 82.22% to 83.56%, while increasing latency and token usage to 3.7x and 2.4x their full-supervision values, respectively. These results support evidence-grounded execution control while identifying a success-cost trade-off in recovery and failure boundaries of heuristic submission rules.
title: Correct Answers, Closed Gates: SolveBind for GUI Agents at the Verification Barrier

summary: v3. For list of changes compared to v2 please see changelog.md in the accompanying zip bundle. ----------------- The $E_8\times\omega E_8$ programme and its companion $SO(3,3)$ BF construction assign a right-chiral origin to pre-gravitation. We distinguish that assignment from parity violation in the observable metric theory. Under the assumptions of a Lorentz-invariant massless spin-2 soft theorem, the leading gravitational coupling is to conserved total energy--momentum; this does not exclude additional mediators or higher-derivative parity-odd effects. Nonrelativistic spin averaging and interface matching provide more limited, separately stated constraints. In a minimally coupled first-order Dirac model the connection is sourced by the spin current, expressible through an axial bilinear, whose presence alone does not violate parity. The displayed broken-phase gravitational and electromagnetic propagation action is parity-even Einstein--Maxwell. We calculate its quadratic tensor evolution and obtain a conditional null result: a parity-symmetric state with parity-symmetric sources has equal helicity powers and vanishing ensemble gravitational $TB/EB$, including tensor-lensing-induced correlations. Explicit Gaussian state families and a sourced-spectrum formula show why the action alone does not select a unique nonzero tensor chirality. We incorporate the chiral-GW lensing mechanism of Xu and Zhang, enforce helicity-power positivity, and perform a convention-matched amplitude audit. Its large flat input cannot be imported into a conventional nearly scale-invariant primordial completion; peaked or late-generated alternatives require their own full transfer and likelihood analysis. The ACT--Planck rotation-template result remains relevant, but its conversion to $g_{\vartheta\gamma}\Delta\vartheta$ applies only to an identified axion--photon component. Spin-force, supernova-timing, and effective-operator bounds are retained with their interaction and astrophysical assumptions. No nonzero parity-odd gravitational coefficient or physical chiral tensor state has yet been derived from the parent programme.
title: Does gravity violate parity? Source currents, screening theorems, and experimental tests of $SU(2)_R$ pre-gravitation

summary: How many members must a committee have before its pairwise majorities can express any collective preference? With enough voters every pattern of pairwise majorities, or tournament, can arise, but a committee of $k$ voters produces only some; for odd $k$, let $N(k)$ be the least number of alternatives on which some tournament arises from no $k$ voters. Only $N(3) = 8$ is known; for five voters our companion paper gave $12 \le N(5) \le 38$ and the first explicit example of moderate size, on 43 vertices. We show $13 \le N(5) \le 22$. The upper bound comes from nine tournaments on 22 vertices that five voters cannot produce: eight one-vertex deletions of doubly regular tournaments on 23 vertices, including every deletion of one of them, and one arc reversal. The Paley tournament on 23 vertices, which Bachmeier et al. (2019) left open after six weeks of SAT solving, is beyond five voters, and so is every other doubly regular tournament on 23 vertices. The lower bound comes from an analysis of all tournaments on 12 vertices. Both doubly regular tournaments on 19 vertices, the Paley tournament and one other, arise from five voters, but not with unit margin, that is, not with every majority carried by three votes to two. The method is a search that places one alternative at a time and exploits the tournament's symmetries; four of the negative results are certified by machine-checkable proofs, and all results are reproducible from a public repository.
title: Tournaments not inducible by five voters

summary: We introduce a Python package called exoVetter that produces vetting metrics and visualizations to evaluate transiting exoplanet signals found in high-cadence time-series photometry. exoVetter is open source, modular, and independent of the mission data so that it can be easily expanded and used as part of different transit search pipelines tuned to different science cases and missions. We demonstrate its use in a pipeline as a way to distinguish real events found in a box-least squares exoplanet transit search of 324,530 light curves from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite mission; we limit our demonstration to stars also observed by the more sensitive Kepler telescope as a way to establish ground truth for the events found in the light curves. Using this ground truth, we provide baseline thresholds for several flux-level vetters and one centroid-offset vetter when using exoVetter metrics on TESS data. Our demonstration also indicates that it is possible to create a planet catalog from the light curves of dim targets (>13.5Tmag) that has a similar fraction of real events to that of the bright targets (<13.5Tmag) for short period events identified in the TESS-Gaia light curves.
title: ExoVetter and a TESS Exoplanet Transit Search of Kepler Stars as Ground Truth

summary: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.
title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery

summary: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite mega-constellations such as Starlink require frequent handovers due to high orbital velocities, resulting in substantial Round-Trip Time (RTT) fluctuations. Accurate RTT prediction can mitigate these fluctuations, yet it fundamentally relies on continuously updated serving- satellite information. Existing serving-satellite identification methods typically complete identification only at the end of each scheduling cycle, creating an identification blind zone that limits real-time prediction. To overcome this limitation, we develop StarRTT, an end-to-end real-time framework that eliminates the blind zone by integrating per-second serving-satellite identification with RTT prediction. Within this framework, we propose Real-Time Long Short-Term Memory (RT-LSTM), an LSTM-based RTT prediction model designed to capture both non-stationary RTT evolution and time-varying geometric relationships among the serving satellite, user terminal, and gateways. Specifically, a historical LSTM encodes historical RTT observations and real-time serving-satellite and gateway-relative features, while a future LSTM processes Two-Line Element (TLE)-propagated future features of the identified serving satellite up to the next scheduling instant. Under strict real-time back-testing, RT-LSTM achieves a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 1.405 ms averaged over all 15 prediction horizons and 15 reference time-slot indices, reducing the error by 4.3 %, 11.6 %, and 22.1 % compared with the existing baseline models, LSTM, StarNet, and Attention-based Spatiotemporal Model (ASTM), respectively. Notably, the reduction over LSTM reaches 12.5 % at the scheduling instant, highlighting the benefit of real-time serving-satellite information when recent RTT observations are limited.
title: StarRTT: An End-to-End Real-Time Framework for Blind Zone-Free RTT Prediction in Starlink LEO Satellite Networks

summary: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task-specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning. We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git
title: Lifelong Context Adaptation through Bidirectional Memory-Skill Learning

summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling.
title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding

summary: This collection provides the code, data, and verification evidence supporting the study “Payment Menu Design for Safe Identification and Recoverable Coverage Deployment” by Jiaming Hu and Cuixia Miao. The study examines payment-menu design for providers with unknown local update rules, jointly requiring safe identification, recovery to ordinary operation, and preservation of the informed benchmarks. The collection contains two complementary archives: • S3_EJOR_Code_Data_v1.0.zip: versioned source code, frozen synthetic inputs and modeled coverage instances derived from public SNDlib topologies, original result ledgers, environment specifications, a data dictionary, mappings between manuscript results and source data, and scripts for rebuilding tables and figures and running verification tests. • S3_EJOR_Full_Evidence_v1.0.zip: retained certificates, verification receipts, execution logs, and failure and timeout records, stored with hash-based deduplication and mappings for restoring their original relative paths. Extract both archives into the same parent directory and follow the README in the Code_Data archive. The public-network instances are modeled coverage and payment scenarios, not observations of real network operations. The external PaGE comparison uses a source-mapped adaptation rather than a successfully built native Storm implementation. All eight extended ten-site tasks passed full V1 verification; seven additional independent audits passed and one timed out. Failed, timed-out, and gated runs are retained and distinguished from completed results. Corresponding author: Jiaming Hu (14438120260091@sdmu.edu.cn).
title: Reproducibility materials for Payment Menu Design for Safe Identification and Recoverable Coverage Deployment

summary: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains an important cause of morbidity and mortality, and simple laboratory markers that identify patients at increased risk may support early clinical risk stratification. Hyponatremia has been associated with neurohormonal activation and adverse outcomes in cardiovascular disease, but its prognostic relevance in patients with ACS requires evaluation in the clinical setting. This prospective single-centre study included 75 patients admitted with ACS to the intensive care unit of Government Royapettah Hospital, Chennai, between April and September 2016. Patients presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset with electrocardiographic evidence of ST-elevation myocardial infarction, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, or unstable angina were enrolled. Patients with previous coronary artery disease, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy or heart failure, previous diuretic use, cirrhosis, hypothyroidism, renal disease, marked renal dysfunction, or refusal to participate were excluded. Serum sodium was measured at admission, 48 hours, and discharge, with sodium <135 mmol/L defining hyponatremia. Patients were followed weekly for 30 days for morbidity and mortality. Nine patients (12.0%) were hyponatremic and 66 (88.0%) were normonatremic. Mean ejection fraction was lower in the hyponatremic group (46.67±7.70%) than in the normonatremic group (53.77±9.96%; p=0.0436), while serum sodium remained significantly lower at all three assessment points (p<0.0001 for each comparison). Killip class also differed significantly between groups (p=0.0461). Adverse in-hospital outcome occurred in 44.44% of hyponatremic patients compared with 10.61% of normonatremic patients (p=0.0071). Thirty-day mortality was 66.67% and 6.06%, respectively (p<0.0001). The reported logistic regression model identified admission, 48-hour, and discharge hyponatremia as significant predictors of mortality. In this cohort, hyponatremia was associated with lower ventricular systolic function, higher clinical severity, adverse in-hospital outcome, and substantially higher 30-day mortality. Serum sodium may therefore provide an accessible prognostic marker in ACS, although confirmation in larger multicentre cohorts is required.

summary: Municipal and rural solid waste management is a multi-stage public service that depends on reliable waste data, source segregation, collection coverage, transport logistics, treatment capacity, recycling markets, institutional coordination and citizen participation. This paper develops an Ahilyanagar District-focused assessment framework informed by the integrated solid waste management perspective described by Abarca Guerrero, Maas, and Hogland (2013), but written independently and adapted to the local administrative context. Official district information lists 16 urban local bodies, while the Ahilyanagar Municipal Corporation reports daily waste generation of approximately 140–150 metric tonnes and an approximate present population of 400,000 for the city. Rahata Municipal Council is listed with a 2011 Census population of 22,335 and an area of 22.74 km². These figures provide a limited baseline, not a complete district waste inventory. The paper proposes a mixed-method approach combining official records, ward-level waste audits, household surveys, stakeholder interviews and statistical analysis. It recommends a district data dashboard, four-stream segregation, decentralised processing where feasible, formal integration of waste pickers, and performance monitoring. Since district-wide measured waste quantities and survey results were not available in the sources reviewed, no unsupported district-wide rates or empirical correlations are claimed.
title: ASSESSING SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT CHALLENGES AND DATA-DRIVEN IMPROVEMENT OPPORTUNITIES IN AHILYANAGAR DISTRICT, MAHARASHTRA, INDIA

Rahata Municipal Council is listed with a 2011 Census population of 22,335 and an area of 22.74 km². These figures provide a limited baseline, not a complete district waste inventory. The paper proposes a mixed-method approach combining official records, ward-level waste audits, household surveys, stakeholder interviews and statistical analysis. It recommends a district data dashboard, four-stream segregation, decentralised processing where feasible, formal integration of waste pickers, and performance monitoring. Since district-wide measured waste quantities and survey results were not available in the sources reviewed, no unsupported district-wide rates or empirical correlations are claimed.
title: ASSESSING SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT CHALLENGES AND DATA-DRIVEN IMPROVEMENT OPPORTUNITIES IN AHILYANAGAR DISTRICT, MAHARASHTRA, INDIA

summary: University technical festivals combine event discovery, registration, payment collection, venue attendance, certification, feedback, and reporting in one workflow, yet they are commonly handled through disconnected forms, spreadsheets, and payment dashboards. This paper presents the design, implementation, and functional verification of Supernova 2.0, a web-based event management platform deployed for the School of Engineering and Technology, MGM University, for a festival held on 4–5 September 2026 with nine flagship competitions. The system is a lightweight PHP/MySQL monolith that binds registration to server-side Razorpay payment verification, records physical venue attendance against the same participant identity, and gates certificate access on that attendance record. Administrative, organizer, and finance duties are separated through role-based access control, and a spreadsheet import path admits offline attendance records. Security controls include CSRF tokens, password hashing, session regeneration, login throttling, prepared statements, security headers, and HMAC signature verification. Validation is functional and workflow-oriented; no performance benchmark, usability study, or penetration test was performed, and no quantitative results are reported. The contribution is the integration of established mechanisms into a single working workflow in a focused, single-event institutional deployment.
title: An Integrated Event Management System for a University

summary: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.
title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning

summary: Contents Folder Contents data/discovery/ Repository metadata and discovery scores for 500 projects. data/analysis/ The 1,500-record human–LLM dataset, 17,180 additional LLM classifications, classification inputs and counts for 117 repositories. data/extraction_used/ Per-repository exports of the analyzed candidates. data/manual_classify/ Master classification sheet and human–LLM comparison sheets. data/survey/ Category-level and demographic survey aggregates. protocol/ Taxonomy categories, LLM instructions, output schema and workbook prompts. scripts/archive/ Repository discovery, historical SATD extraction and LLM classification scripts. provenance/mining_logs/ Compressed SATD extraction logs. results/computed/ RQ1 and RQ2 counts, repository distributions, false-positive counts and RQ3 aggregates. figures/ AI-CPS taxonomy and practitioner criticality figures. survey/ Practitioner questionnaire. Setup Install Python and Git. Open a terminal in the folder containing requirements.txt , then install the Python dependencies: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt Repository discovery Run the discovery script to generate a repository metadata CSV: python scripts/archive/discover_repositories_original.py --output repos_for_satd.csv --max-repos 500 --include-readme The command exports up to 500 repositories and includes README inspection. Other available settings are listed with: python scripts/archive/discover_repositories_original.py --help For authenticated GitHub requests, set the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable before running the script. Historical SATD extraction Run the miner on the supplied repository list: python scripts/archive/mine_satd_original.py --input data/discovery/repos_for_satd.csv --output-dir satd_results --repo-cache tmp_repos --log-dir satd_logs --since-year 2022 The script traverses available commits from the specified year, retrieves marker-bearing deleted source lines and their available pre-change context, and writes per-repository CSV files and logs. tmp_repos is the script's temporary clone directory. LLM classification In scripts/archive/llm_classification.py , replace the input, output and sample-count placeholders. For example, to classify the additional input: INPUT_FILE = r"data/analysis/additional_input_17180.csv" OUTPUT_FILE = r"new_additional_llm_results.csv" MAX_SAMPLES = 17180 To use the initial subset instead, set INPUT_FILE to data/analysis/manual_input_1500.csv and MAX_SAMPLES to 1500 . The sample count must be an integer. Set the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, then run: python scripts/archive/llm_classification.py The script reads ID , SATD_Keyword , SATD_Comment , Context_Type and Context_Code , and saves broad classifications, AI-CPS categories and proposed category names. Checkpoints are saved beside the output. To resume an interrupted run, use the same input, settings and output path. Results The supplied summaries are in results/computed/ . RQ1 percentages exclude false positives; RQ2 percentages use the AI-CPS-specific total within each analysis. Figures are supplied as PDFs in figures/ .
title: Replication Package of the Paper: "Self-Admitted Technical Debt in AI-Intensive Cyber-Physical Systems: An Empirical Study"

summary: CSE-Sp: Spanish adaptation of the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale Analysis materials and supplemental material This repository contains the analysis materials and the supplemental material for a psychometric validation study of the Spanish adaptation of the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale (CSE-Sp) in a sample of 503 university students. FILES   CSE-Sp_supplemental_material.docx       Supplemental Material S1 to S13 cited in the manuscript (19 tables).   cse_sp_analysis.R       Complete analysis script, organized in the order of the manuscript:       item analysis, outlier screening, random split, exploratory and       confirmatory factor analyses, bifactor indices, estimator sensitivity       (WLSMV), cross-validation, reliability, measurement invariance by sex,       disciplinary area and institution, MIMIC model, sensitivity analysis       excluding participants older than 30, convergent, criterion and       discriminant validity, and the item-level comparison with the original       and Turkish versions.   cse_sp_export_matrices.R       Script used to generate the correlation matrices deposited here.   matrix_halfA_polychoric.csv       Polychoric correlation matrix of the 20 items, half A (n = 253).       Input of the primary exploratory factor analysis.   matrix_halfA_pearson.csv       Product-moment correlation matrix of the 20 items, half A (n = 253).       Input of the replication reported in parallel.   matrix_total_pearson.csv       Product-moment correlation matrix of the 20 items, total sample       (N = 503). SOFTWARE ENVIRONMENT   R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24 ucrt), platform x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64,   running under Windows 11 x64.   Packages: psych 2.6.5, lavaan 0.6-21, semTools 0.5-8, MVN 6.3,   readxl 1.5.0, mnormt 2.1.2, pbivnorm 0.6.0, quadprog 1.5-8.   Seed used for the stratified random split of the sample and for the   bootstrap confidence intervals: 2026. The split assigns 253 cases to   half A (exploratory analyses) and 250 to half B (confirmatory analyses). WHAT CAN AND CANNOT BE REPRODUCED FROM THESE FILES The deposited correlation matrices reproduce the sampling-adequacy indices (KMO, Bartlett), the exploratory factor analysis on both the polychoric and the product-moment matrix, the factor-retention criteria (parallel analysis, MAP, VSS, eigenvalue ratio), and the internal-consistency coefficients computed on standardized items. They do not reproduce the confirmatory factor analyses, the bifactor indices, the cross-validation, or the measurement-invariance and MIMIC models. These were estimated with robust maximum likelihood (MLR), which requires individual response data in order to compute the robust corrections to the fit statistics and standard errors. The same applies to the validity correlations, which were computed on subsets of participants with varying sample sizes. The analysis script documents every one of these analyses so that they can be reproduced on the individual data. ACCESS TO THE INDIVIDUAL DATA The individual response data are not deposited here. They were collected within an institutional assessment program and their ownership lies with the institution rather than with the research team. Both input files used by the analysis script (cse_sp_full_sample.xlsx and cse_sp_validity_subset.xlsx) are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. LICENSE CC BY 4.0

SOFTWARE ENVIRONMENT   R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24 ucrt), platform x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64,   running under Windows 11 x64.   Packages: psych 2.6.5, lavaan 0.6-21, semTools 0.5-8, MVN 6.3,   readxl 1.5.0, mnormt 2.1.2, pbivnorm 0.6.0, quadprog 1.5-8.   Seed used for the stratified random split of the sample and for the   bootstrap confidence intervals: 2026. The split assigns 253 cases to   half A (exploratory analyses) and 250 to half B (confirmatory analyses). WHAT CAN AND CANNOT BE REPRODUCED FROM THESE FILES The deposited correlation matrices reproduce the sampling-adequacy indices (KMO, Bartlett), the exploratory factor analysis on both the polychoric and the product-moment matrix, the factor-retention criteria (parallel analysis, MAP, VSS, eigenvalue ratio), and the internal-consistency coefficients computed on standardized items. They do not reproduce the confirmatory factor analyses, the bifactor indices, the cross-validation, or the measurement-invariance and MIMIC models. These were estimated with robust maximum likelihood (MLR), which requires individual response data in order to compute the robust corrections to the fit statistics and standard errors. The same applies to the validity correlations, which were computed on subsets of participants with varying sample sizes. The analysis script documents every one of these analyses so that they can be reproduced on the individual data. ACCESS TO THE INDIVIDUAL DATA The individual response data are not deposited here. They were collected within an institutional assessment program and their ownership lies with the institution rather than with the research team. Both input files used by the analysis script (cse_sp_full_sample.xlsx and cse_sp_validity_subset.xlsx) are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. LICENSE CC BY 4.0

summary: Nepal’s Constitution of 2015 protects dignity, personal liberty, peaceful assembly and constitutional remedies. Yet investigations into the 2015 Terai protests and the September 2025 Gen Z uprising expose a persistent gap between rights and the use of state coercion. This paper argues that the gap is best understood through an accountability chain: broad public-order powers, qualified protection for official acts, evidentiary dependence and uncertain institutional implementation. The analysis focuses on sections 35, 37 and 38 of the Police Act, 2012 B.S. (1955 C.E.), sections 6, 6A and 6B of the Local Administration Act, 2028 B.S. (1971 C.E.) and Nepal’s duties under the ICCPR and Convention against Torture. Through doctrinal analysis, a source-critical reconstruction of protest events, peer-reviewed scholarship and carefully delimited comparative jurisprudence, the article separates contemporaneous death counts from later totals, inquiry recommendations from court judgments and state violence from crimes by other actors. It incorporates the 2026 inquiry and National Human Rights Commission findings, one-year anniversary reporting and the October 2026 review of protest-related criminal cases. Its central contribution is a rights-consistent and measurable program for controlling force, preserving evidence, independently investigating deaths and protecting remedies without undermining legitimate public safety.
title: Constitutional Liberty and Protest Policing: A Comparative Perspective on Structural Impunity, Gen Z Dissent and Accountability Reform in Nepal Doctrinal and comparative legal research

summary: Implementation and reproducibility package for static and fixed-ion time-dependent Berry-phase electric fields in SIESTA, by Javier Junquera. This is a new version of the reproducibility record supporting the invited Philosophical Transactions A manuscript "Insulating solids in finite electric fields: implementation and validation in SIESTA" (RSTA-2026-0113). The package supplies the exact source revision and pinned dependency sources, the 61-page technical report and editable LaTeX with figures, complete 53-routine Doxygen HTML and printable API, the User Guide, three progressive tutorials, documented calculation inputs and outputs, raw accepted and failed validation campaigns, source/executable/input hashes, CPU/wall/RSS measurements, and portable reproduction and plotting instructions. Validation covers serial, MPI, OpenMP and hybrid execution, static forces/stress, collinear and NC/SOC spin including the documented U/J path, fixed-ion real-time propagation, empty-owner and unsupported-input checks, and matched disabled-feature overhead. Four fresh exact-input SIESTA fields replay the earlier reference calculations; independent ABINIT results are reanalysed from preserved raw outputs, not newly calculated. The evidence is single-host and configuration-specific; unsupported, untested and unavailable combinations and convergence/scaling limits are documented. Read the technical report (PDF) . Start with README.md for extraction, checksums, build/test commands and scientific reproduction. Each archive has a per-file SHA-256 inventory. The six prepared implementation commits were pushed through 3365997ba; MR 570 metadata remains held for the owner final check. New scientific data, documentation, original figures and code are GNU GPL version 3 only (GPL-3.0-only), matching the official SIESTA licence . The earlier reference subset retains its CC BY 4.0 data/documentation and GPLv3-or-later script terms. SIESTA dependencies, documentation assets and PSML pseudopotentials retain their individual notices and provenance; see LICENSES.md and COPYING. Dated licence-hold statements in the immutable evidence predate the owner instruction of 26 October 2026. The preceding complete 84-case archive remains available as DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23315274 ; it is not duplicated here. The included exact subset supports the documented independent replay. This work is part of Grant PID2022-139776NB-C63, funded by MICIU/AEI/10.13039/501100011033 and by ERDF/EU.
title: Finite electric fields in SIESTA: implementation and compliance validation

summary: The covering number $C(v,k,t)$ is the least number of $k$-subsets, called blocks, of a $v$-set such that every $t$-subset lies in one of them. We reduce the question whether a covering with $L$ blocks exists to the classification of links. If every point of such a covering lies in at least $r$ blocks and $(r+1)v>kL$, some point lies in exactly $r$ blocks, and its link, the blocks through it with the point removed, is a $(v-1,k-1,t-1)$-covering with $r$ blocks. It then suffices to list these links up to isomorphism, to prove the list complete, and to show that no link in the list extends to a covering with $L$ blocks. Completeness is certified by one unsatisfiable formula that excludes the listed classes, so the program that lists the links need not be trusted. In general the last two steps are decided by propositional satisfiability (SAT) solving, with every formula written by two separately implemented encoders and every refutation checked by a formally verified proof checker. For links with four blocks and $t=3$ we give the classification by hand, under a condition on the parameters. As an application we determine twenty-five covering numbers with $t\in\{3,4,5\}$ in which the published lower bound was one less than the size of a known covering, among them $C(39,24,3)=9$.
title: Links of minimum degree and exact covering numbers

summary: The same upper central incisor in every panel, cut from the lip side to the palate side, with the gum, ligament and bone around it. The tooth and the tissues at its neck are drawn to published measurements; the break, the etched enamel, the key and the layers show what typically happens, not one patient's tooth. Sources The rebuild follows two principles from one textbook. The additive principle: in a direct restoration the etching and bonding are extended beyond the defect onto intact enamel, to blend and reinforce the restoration; its example is a small chipped edge restored without preparation: the tooth was etched, bonded and restored well beyond the fracture line under rubber dam. And natural guided stratification: a silicone index made from a wax-up or mock-up holds a palatal shell of enamel-like material, dentine-like increments are placed where the natural dentine was, and the last increment is the labial enamel. Magne and Belser 2022, Biomimetic Restorative Dentistry, volume 1, pages 319, 330 and 331. In 455 crown-fractured permanent incisors followed for a mean of 2.3 years and up to 17, the pulp survived in 99 per cent of teeth the injury had not also loosened or displaced, and in none of them did it die; when the tooth had also been loosened, pulp death in fractures through enamel and dentine, like this one, rose from 0 to 28 per cent. Robertson et al. 2000, International Journal of Paediatric Dentistry. https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-263x.2000.00191.x A 2024 German clinical guideline on direct composite restorations, agreed by strong consensus, recommends etching the enamel of every direct composite restoration with phosphoric acid, to improve the long-term quality of the enamel margin and prevent discoloration there. It finds both rubber dam and other isolation workable, with rubber dam possibly helping restorations last longer. These process recommendations are consensus-based. Sekundo et al. 2024, The Journal of Adhesive Dentistry, part 2. https://doi.org/10.3290/j.jad.b5749192 Acid on the enamel only, before a universal adhesive: in a randomised trial of 295 back-tooth fillings in 70 patients, fillings bonded this way showed significantly fewer defects at their edges after 24 months than those bonded with the adhesive alone. Barceleiro et al. 2023, Journal of Applied Oral Science. https://doi.org/10.1590/1678-7757-2022-0323 In fillings at the necks of teeth, a meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials found less staining and fewer adaptation defects at the edges when the enamel was etched selectively before a self-etch adhesive, and fewer fillings lost at three years. Szesz et al. 2016, Journal of Dentistry, systematic review and meta-analysis. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdent.2016.05.009 A Cochrane review of six randomised trials with 1,342 participants found low-certainty evidence that rubber dam may lower the failure rate of fillings compared with cotton rolls at six months, and very uncertain evidence at other times; all the trials were at high risk of bias, and the results came from fillings at the necks of teeth and in children's back teeth. Miao et al. 2021, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009858.pub3 A meta-analysis of 21 prospective clinical trials of front-tooth composites estimated that 90 per cent of Class IV restorations, which rebuild a broken corner or edge of a front tooth, last 10 years without being replaced; bulk fracture was the main reason for replacement, more often with microfilled composites. Twelve of the trials started before 1991. Heintze, Rousson and Hickel 2015, Dental Materials. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dental.2015.01.015 A critical appraisal of clinical and laboratory publications: a bevel on the enamel margin was traditionally placed for retention and a gradual colour transition, but modern adhesives, composites and technique make adequate front-tooth composites possible without one, with a more conservative preparation, a smaller restored
title: Bonding a Chipped Front Tooth: Composite Layers, Step by Step

summary: Resumen Introducción y objetivo: La disfagia asociada a la patología tiroidea puede preceder al tratamiento, aparecer tras la cirugía o relacionarse con radioyodo, radioterapia y terapias sistémicas. Este trabajo revisa sus mecanismos, evaluación y rehabilitación, con especial atención al cáncer de tiroides y a la intervención logopédica y miofuncional. Método: Se realizó una revisión dirigida de literatura biomédica accesible, principalmente de 2015–2026, y una integración crítica de materiales docentes. Se distinguió entre evidencia específica de cáncer tiroideo, evidencia procedente de cirugía tiroidea general y extrapolación desde otras etiologías de disfagia. Resultados: La disfagia tiroidea es multifactorial y puede combinar compresión o invasión aerodigestiva, lesión neural, edema, adherencias, fibrosis, alteración del esfínter esofágico superior y toxicidad salival. Los síntomas tempranos tras tiroidectomía son frecuentes y generalmente transitorios, pero la persistencia, la pérdida ponderal, la disfonía, la tos ineficaz o el deterioro respiratorio y nutricional requieren evaluación específica. La laringoscopia, FEES y VFSS aportan información complementaria. La rehabilitación debe dirigirse al fenotipo demostrado, con objetivos medibles y reevaluación. Conclusiones: No existe una intervención universal. La práctica segura exige línea basal, evaluación longitudinal, selección de pruebas por la pregunta clínica, tratamiento etiológico cuando proceda y uso selectivo de compensaciones, terapia miofuncional y rehabilitación de voz, tos y deglución. Palabras clave: Trastornos de Deglución, Neoplasias de la Tiroides, Enfermedades de la Tiroides, Tiroidectomía, Rehabilitación, Calidad de Vida Summary Background and objective: Dysphagia related to thyroid disease may precede treatment, develop after surgery, or result from radioiodine, external radiotherapy, and systemic therapies. This review examines its mechanisms, assessment, and rehabilitation, focusing on thyroid cancer and speech-language and orofacial myofunctional management. Methods: A targeted review of accessible biomedical literature, mainly from 2015 to 2026, was combined with a critical integration of teaching materials. Evidence specific to thyroid cancer was distinguished from general thyroid surgery evidence and extrapolation from other dysphagia populations. Results: Thyroid-related dysphagia is multifactorial and may involve aerodigestive compression or invasion, neural injury, edema, adhesions, fibrosis, upper esophageal sphincter dysfunction, and salivary toxicity. Early symptoms after thyroidectomy are common and usually transient; persistent symptoms, weight loss, dysphonia, ineffective cough, or respiratory and nutritional deterioration require targeted assessment. Laryngoscopy, FEES, and VFSS provide complementary information. Rehabilitation should address the demonstrated phenotype through measurable goals and reassessment. Conclusions: No universal intervention is appropriate. Safe practice requires baseline assessment, longitudinal follow-up, test selection according to the clinical question, etiological treatment when indicated, and selective use of compensation, myofunctional therapy, and voice-cough-swallow rehabilitation. Keywords: Deglutition Disorders, Thyroid Neoplasms, Thyroid Diseases, Thyroidectomy, Rehabilitation, Quality of Life
title: Enfermedades de tiroides y disfagia: mecanismos, evaluación y rehabilitación basada en evidencia | Thyroid Diseases and Dysphagia: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Evidence-Based Rehabilitation

summary: Data and replication package for the systematic literature review "Lifecycle Assurance for AI-Enabled Clinical Software: A Systematic Literature Review", submitted to Information and Software Technology. The review covers 141 independent studies (94 primary-practice and 47 framework studies) published between January 2019 and 17 August 2026, identified through Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, PubMed and a citation-chasing audit. Files: - README.md: overview, codes used and instructions for reproducing the results. - Lifecycle_Assurance_Data.xlsx: study-level workbook with the included studies, search strings, codebook, extraction and appraisal data, requirement-to-evidence mappings, agreement data and LAEC records. Start with the README sheet. - Supplementary_Material.pdf: supplementary material of the article (Tables S1 to S15). - replication_package.zip: database search strings, the coded data as CSV files and a Python script (standard library only) that recomputes every count reported in the article. Version 1.1.0 corresponds to the submitted manuscript and replaces the earlier version.
title: Lifecycle Assurance for AI-Enabled Clinical Software: A Systematic Literature Review (Data and Replication Package)

summary: Reference inventory, Sentinel-1 product lists, detector outputs, scoring tables, robustness tests and code behind the paper "Can open radar see war damage? A placebo-controlled validation of Sentinel-1 coherence and backscatter change detection at Iranian strike sites, 2025–2026" (Raj Kumar Mishra, submitted to Science of Remote Sensing, October 2026). The deposit holds the 39-entry geolocated reference inventory with its sources; the 312 Sentinel-1 scene pairs and HyP3 processing options (79 war-period, 107 placebo, 66 burst and 60 summer-2026 products); cluster, score and placebo-comparison tables of the coherence-drop detector at eight settings; backscatter change-point rasters and scores for every site and window, with no-strike windows one, two and three years before each war; Sentinel-2 and LISS-IV optical checks; VIIRS fire (NASA FIRMS records), night-light, TROPOMI, MODIS, Landsat, OCO-2/3, lidar and EMIT before/after tests with the positive control in Russia and Crimea; the pass-timing tables; the six places found by the method with their source checks; the robustness tests (placebo transplant, empirical null, holdout and others), with the rules of the further tests, set before they were run; the PWTT baseline (separate file pwtt_baseline_v1.0.0.zip); and the Python and Earth Engine scripts. Original satellite products are not included (except the NASA FIRMS fire detections used for the fire tests; the others are open and can be regenerated as described in README.md); derived rasters, image views and tables are, and contain modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2022–2026). Access is restricted and granted on request for research use; code (09_code): BSD 3-Clause. MANIFEST.csv lists every file with MD5 and SHA-256.
title: Data and code for "Can open radar see war damage? A placebo-controlled validation of Sentinel-1 coherence and backscatter change detection at Iranian strike sites, 2025–2026"

summary: This repository contains the full research artifact for a comparative study of automated issue labeling in the Qiskit ecosystem. The project focuses on assigning GitHub issues to a domain-specific taxonomy of quantum software modules using multiple modeling paradigms: classical machine learning baselines, fine-tuned transformer models, direct prompting with large language models, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The work is designed to support reproducible evaluation of AI-assisted bug triage and taxonomy-driven issue classification in a specialized scientific software repository. The dataset and experiments are organized around the issue-labeling task described in README.md. The repository includes the annotated issue corpus in qiskit_repo_quantum_issues.json, baseline and exploratory analysis in Analysis, transformer training pipelines in Fine_tuned_Experiments, direct GPT prompting experiments in Gpt_Experiments, and retrieval-based pipelines in RAG_Experiments. Output artifacts include trained model results, prediction arrays, confusion metrics, per-label performance summaries, and experiment logs stored alongside each experiment family. ### Repository structure - qiskit_repo_quantum_issues.json: Qiskit issue dataset used for training and evaluation. - Analysis: baseline models and analysis scripts, including:   - ml_baselines.py: TF-IDF logistic regression and linear SVM baselines   - quantum_term_analysis.py: analysis of quantum-domain terminology   - bot_labeling_analysis.py: bot-vs-human labeling analysis   - predictions: saved predictions and evaluation outputs - Fine_tuned_Experiments: fine-tuned transformer experiments with scripts and results:   - DistilBERT.py   - Roberta.py   - result folders such as DistilBERT_results and Roberta_results - Gpt_Experiments: zero-shot and few-shot prompting experiments with OpenAI models:   - scripts containing model-specific prompt scripts   - output folders for prompt results and predictions - RAG_Experiments: retrieval-augmented and agentic RAG pipelines   - code: experiment scripts for zeroshot, few-shot, adaptive, and direct generation pipelines - LICENSE: MIT license - README.md: project overview and usage guide
title: Automated Quantum Issue Labeling in Qiskit: Large Language Models and Fine-Tuned Transformers

summary: Abstract A dimensionless closure relation associated with the five-constant system {e_c, m_e, h, c, G} predicts the frequency ν_zp = 0.0605390 Hz. The same scale has the equivalent laboratory representations τ_zp ≈ 16.5183 s, ν_zp = 0.06053898(67) Hz, ℓ_zp ≈ 10.9614 cm. The present paper formulates a metrological test of this prediction. An admissible determination must identify one of these quantities through an independently observed physical phenomenon rather than calculate it from the closure relation or from an algebraically equivalent expression. In particular, the predicted value must not enter the apparatus, calibration chain, or analysis through G or through any quantity whose numerical value has itself been fixed from the closure. The target follows from α_eG · hν_zp/(m_ec²) = 1, with α_eG = e_c/(m_e√G), which links the electron–gravitational dimensionless sector to the electron Compton frequency. The dimensional origin of the three-member structure {α, α_eG, η_j}, with η_j = hν_j/(m_ec²), is developed in a companion paper, where the closure is proposed as a physical conjecture. An independent realization would provide a direct experimental test of the proposed closure and, within the framework, an alternative route to the gravitational constant, G = [e_chν_zp/(m_e²c²)]². The problem is therefore reduced to a specific metrological question with defined numerical targets, independence criteria, uncertainty propagation, and falsification conditions.
title: Metrological Test of a Predicted Closure Scale at 0.0605390 Hz: Frequency, Period, Velocity, and Length Realizations

summary: This preprint examines how space-themed socioscientific issues (SSI) connect scientific understanding with social and ethical judgment, and how these connections can inform science and STEM education. Drawing on 1,316 educational reports—58 space-related and 1,258 non-space-related—the review combines comparative mapping with detailed examination of space contexts. It addresses four interconnected areas: the representation and educational forms of space-themed SSI; disciplinary knowledge and reasoning; historical, present and future perspectives; and teaching approaches, student responses and learning outcomes. The evidence encompasses learner research, curriculum and teacher education, educational reviews and supporting contributions. Manuscript.pdf — Complete preprint manuscript. Presents the conceptual framework, review methods, findings across the four research questions, discussion, educational implications and references. All main-text figures and tables are included. Word and HTML copies, if supplied, are alternative formats of the same manuscript. S1_Methods_and_Evidence_Tables.pdf — Supplementary methods and selected evidence tables. Explains the search and selection procedures, eligibility criteria, analytical units, coding definitions and weighting methods. It also documents temporal reconstruction and sensitivity analyses, selected science–society reasoning cases, pedagogical evidence, quantitative comparisons and source-identification qualifications. S2_Report_Evidence_Catalogue.html — Searchable report evidence catalogue. Provides searchable and filterable report-level information, including educational scope, Earth–space connections, disciplinary knowledge, epistemic reasoning, teaching practices, outcomes and temporal interpretation. Bibliographic references, source links and selection reasons connect the synthesis to its supporting evidence. Download and open the file in a web browser. S3_Analysis_Data.xlsx — Analysis data workbook. Contains 26 worksheets documenting search strategies, selection decisions, report characteristics, coding definitions, teaching and outcome evidence, temporal coordinates and model parameters, relationships between reports, and the distributions underlying the analyses.
title: Distant Worlds, Shared Questions: A Systematic Review of Space-Themed Socioscientific Education

Twenty-eight tests pass in each Python mode, with ten deliberate rejection runs. No discrepancy was found in this finite ingredient. This is finite computational verification and scoped AI review, not a kernel proof or human peer review. The characteristic-zero lifting, simultaneous real-form/genericity argument, real PSD deformation and final nonliftability theorem remain outside scope. summary: HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides horizontal box detection, evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, an interactive annotation viewer, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API. 📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/hbb2obb , with a quick start on the bundled sample data, a guide per command, pages on how the conversion works, the confidence score, the metrics and provenance, and a CLI and API reference generated from the code. Why HBB2OBB 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs : prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required. 🚗 No HBBs? Detect them : the hbb2obb-detect command runs an Ultralytics detector over the images and writes the horizontal boxes the conversion consumes, confidence column included. 🧩 Model ensemble : combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results. 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe : region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, a mask split by an occluder is fitted back together, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found, counted and reported rather than left to be discovered afterwards. 🔎 Confidence-scored output : every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the scores go in the label files or in a side-car directory that keeps them strictly standard, and the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score. 📐 Flexible scaling : positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations. 📊 Evaluate and optimize : evaluation against ground truth on IoU, orientation error, and the share of boxes above a high IoU bar, plus the hbb2obb-optimize command, a hyperparameter search over SAM inference resolution, scale factors, and morphological opening kernel, driven by a configuration file so that a whole benchmark of model ensembles is a single reproducible command. 🔬 Where the score comes from : the hbb2obb-analyze command breaks one evaluation down by the ground truth's orientation, size, frame edge, difficulty and class, and scores the conversion against emitting the horizontal prompt unchanged. 🔄 Five annotation formats : read and write YOLO, DOTA, Pascal VOC, COCO, and LabelMe, for horizontal and oriented boxes alike, with a check that proves every format encodes the same boxes. 🔍 Interactive viewer : the hbb2obb-view command pans and zooms over the annotations, in any format, coloring boxes by confidence and overlaying predictions against ground truth. Where a set ships the same boxes several ways, it names the format on screen and switches between them on a keypress. Features HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation, written in absolute pixels or, with --normalize , relative to [0, 1], the convention Ultralytics reads. HBB detection : produce the horizontal boxes in the first place with any Ultralytics detector, a local file, a link, the Ultralytics catalogue, or Hugging Face, passing any other predictor argument straight through. Multiple model support : SAM, SAM2, SAM2.1, SAM3, Mobile SAM, and FastSAM families. Model ensemble via majority voting for enhanced accuracy. Confidence scoring : a per-OBB quali
title: HBB2OBB: Horizontal to Oriented Bounding Box Conversion and Evaluation Tool

summary: Bounded Agentic Distribution Experiments (v0.7.0): A Reproducible Framework for Comparing Agentic Intervention Discovery with Non-Agentic Search This software implements the computational framework and pre-pilot experimental protocol associated with the research manuscript Evaluating the Incremental Value of Agentic Intervention Discovery over Non-Agentic Search in Multi-Actor Distribution Networks . The framework evaluates whether a generative AI agent can identify economically beneficial operational interventions beyond those discovered by budget-matched non-agentic search. Agentic and non-agentic methods operate within the same typed intervention space, access the same simulator information, and are subject to common evaluation budgets. Candidate interventions undergo deterministic verification of encoded structural constraints and, where applicable, stochastic qualification against economic, service, route, and actor-participation criteria. The reference environment represents a stylized print-media distribution network with 420 retailers, 18 baseline delivery vehicles, uncertain demand, allocation decisions, reverse logistics, route constraints, temporary fleet capacity, discontinuous staffing requirements, and sales-contingent remuneration. Its parameters combine industry-informed inputs, documented benchmarks, modeling assumptions, and calibration targets. The environment is intended for controlled computational evaluation rather than empirical representation of the Italian distribution industry. Experimental design Version 0.7.0 implements two frozen intervention-complexity regimes: Low-complexity regime (RL): allocation reweighting only, with a maximum intervention length of one action. Multi-domain coupled regime (RC): allocation, route transfer, temporary fleet, and forecasting interventions, with a maximum intervention length of three actions. Both regimes use a candidate-evaluation budget of 40 simulator calls. The primary comparison uses ten independent generative-agent realizations and ten independent simulated-annealing realizations per regime. The software separates proposal-mechanism randomness from simulation-scenario randomness and supports common random numbers for comparative evaluation. The statistical implementation includes regime-specific pilot sizing, independent within-method repetition resampling, shared scenario resampling, and a two-dimensional bootstrap for confirmatory inference. Final-test selection follows a frozen rule combining precision requirements from both regimes with the minimum-detectable-effect requirement for the multi-domain superiority hypothesis. Software contents The archive includes the Python simulator and experimental orchestration code, command-line interface, frozen configuration files, typed intervention specifications, agent prompt and structured-output schemas, statistical analysis procedures, automated tests, freeze manifest, calibration documentation, and four Jupyter notebooks covering protocol execution, pilot sizing, repeated experiments, and economic calibration. Validation and research status The implementation passes 31 automated software and protocol-consistency tests. These tests examine computational correctness, reproducibility, regime restrictions, seed handling, bootstrap procedures, and experimental locking. They do not establish empirical agent performance. This release corresponds to the frozen pre-pilot protocol BAD-420-v0.7-2026-09-11 . The final-test set remains locked until a valid pilot mechanically determines its size. No live API-based agent-performance experiment or confirmatory comparison is included in this release. Consequently, the software does not establish that agentic intervention discovery outperforms, matches, or underperforms non-agentic search. The purpose of this release is to make the computational model, methodological assumptions, experimental controls, and pre-result evaluation protocol available for independent inspection, repl
title: Agentic_distribution_experiments_v0.7_pre_pilot_with_notebooks

summary: This dataset contains 530,132 method-level provenance relationships, each annotated with the source and sink licenses, license compatibility classification, and supporting metadata, mined across a large corpus of GitHub repositories. It is the full, unfiltered version of the empirical corpus used in an anonymous submission on method-level license compliance debt, currently under double-blind peer review. This file is hosted on Zenodo rather than GitHub solely because of GitHub's 100MB per-file limit; it is not a separate or reduced dataset. A smaller, GitHub-hosted sample ( downsized_compliance_empirical_dataset.csv ) and the full replication package, including the classification engine, validation data, and analysis notebooks, are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EmpiricalStudyPaper-842E/ . Schema : organization_name , hash , source_method_name , sink_method_name , source_repository_url , sink_repository_url , source_file_location , sink_file_location , source_query_project , violation . Full column documentation is in the replication package's README. Anonymity note : this dataset is uploaded under an anonymous identity for double-blind review. Author information will be added in a future version of this deposit upon acceptance, under the same DOI. License : CC-BY 4.0.
title: Full Compliance Empirical Dataset: Method-Level License Reuse and Compliance Relationships

summary: We conduct a version-pinned, reproducible forensic audit of the public Einstein Elevator data package (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.15167723) to determine whether it supports validation of quantum sensor certificates. Through an exhaustive cross-file sliding-window correlation search over 44,207,922 comparisons and exact six-decimal rounding checks, we find that all 31 exported sensor channels have a unique best match within the enumerated raw traces under the stated protocol. Residual numerical differences are highly consistent with text-based absolute quantization; the correlation-loss approximation 1 - r ≈ δ² / (24σx²) is diagnostic for this dataset, not a universal proof. We inspect the MATLAB-derived 318-point population series and reconcile it with a 2022 workbook entry only at the level of counts. An archive-wide search of 181 file objects and 1,654 MATLAB metadata fields finds no documented join key linking the 2022 run-indexed population series to the 2017 timestamped traces under the enumerated search protocol. Using Fréchet-Hoeffding bounds and a Charnes-Cooper linearization, we establish that the public archive does not supply the joint observations needed to identify the EKF false-safe risk without additional coupling assumptions; the formal program is illustrative and is not populated with empirical failure/acceptance coefficients because the required linked observations are absent. We frame this as a bounded data-contract limitation for downstream statistical validation, not as a failure of the original experiment.
title: A Reproducible Provenance Audit of the Public Einstein Elevator Data Package: Trace Correspondence, Metadata Linkage, and the Non-Identifiability of Sensor-Certificate Risk from the Public Archive

CAUSAL INFERENCE AND CLINICAL EVIDENCE ENGINEERING FOR INTELLIGENT NANO-ACUPUNCTURE AT THE LIMIT STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW EPOCH / FLAGSHIP 25 OF 90 777-PAGE NONCLINICAL RESEARCH WORKING EDITION v1.0 / 2026 This 777-page STARLI flagship volume develops a falsifiable research program for causal inference and clinical evidence engineering in the proposed field of intelligent nano-acupuncture. It is an architecture for future study, not a report of a performed clinical trial. The core three-coupling is intelligent acupuncture, causal inference and evidence engineering. The central question is whether any prespecified patient-important outcome difference between an explicitly defined stimulation strategy and a credible sham comparator can be identified without confounding, unmasking, outcome selection, differential care or inappropriate inference from engineering demonstrations. The candidate causal estimand is ATE = E[Y|do(stim)] - E[Y|do(sham)] when the interventions, target population, outcome scale, follow-up, and identifying assumptions have been explicitly defined. This expression is not evidence by itself. The work distinguishes physical phantom measurements, AI model performance, sensor quality and procedural safety from actual randomized human evidence. It examines why tactile sham procedures may have nonzero effects and why expectancy, practitioner attention, natural history, regression to the mean, missing follow-up and differing intervention versions can imitate a device-specific benefit. Thirty distinct mathematical and methodological plates include potential outcomes, g-formula standardization, inverse-propensity weighting, augmented doubly robust estimation, imbalance diagnostics, absolute harm contrasts, cluster design effects, intention-to-treat, treatment-by-contact interactions, longitudinal comparisons, selection bias, sensitivity analysis for missing data, sample-size planning, noninferiority, multiplicity, sequential testing, meta-analytic heterogeneity, Bayesian sensitivity and policy-value limits. Formula applications state their assumptions, variables and units and suggest tests that could falsify invalid transfers. These are established analytic methods used as research tools, not original scientific laws.

summary: This artifact reproduces the evaluation of DrNLA, a method that rewrites non-linear integer arithmetic (NLA) expressions in program branch/loop guards into equivalent linear integer arithmetic (LIA) via context-dependent dual rewriting, enabling off-the-shelf LIA-based CTL verifiers (T2, FuncTion) to verify branching-time properties of NLA programs. Contents: the DrNLA implementation (src/); all benchmark suites (benchmarks/: ctl-svcomp, ctl-pldi13small, custom, real-world, and the 320-instance ctl-diverse suite); the CIL source instrumenter (deps/dyn_instr/, prebuilt binary + source); the reproduction drivers, pinned-toolchain manifest, and reference results (reproduce/); and the context-experiment inputs. Reproduced tables: Tab. 1 (NLA->LIA rewrite results), Tab. 2 (context necessity / reach-ctx), and Tab. 3/4 (T2 and FuncTion enabled by DrNLA). Usage: unzip and follow REPRODUCE.md (the single entry point); exact pinned toolchain is in reproduce/MANIFEST.md. The external verifiers — DIG (commit a6a4d04), Ultimate Automizer 0.2.2, T2 (10f1373), and FuncTion (bdeeae1) — are obtained and built per deps/README.md; DIG must be a6a4d04 (newer DIG changes the invariant-generator flags). All reported numbers were produced on a single Ubuntu 22.04 workstation with a 900 s per-benchmark timeout.

title: DrNLA: Context-dependent linearization for CTL verification of non-linear arithmetic programs (Reproduction Artifact)

summary: Overview This dataset comprises X-ray CT projection data of a composite plate. The data were acquired in 2009 at beamline I12 of the Diamond Light Source. A total of 5401 projection images were collected with an angular step of 0.033° (180°/5400). The dataset exhibits several imaging issues, making it a useful test case for preprocessing and artefact-correction algorithms: random bright pixels caused by electron scattering, ring artefacts often caused by bright defects on the scintillator, unknown optical distortion, and a possible small tilt of the sample. Image Specifications Projection image dimensions: 4008 × 1000 pixels Acquisition Sequence and Calibration Data - Projections : 5401 images, acquired with an angular step of 0.033° (180°/5400) - Dark-field images : 10 images -  Flat-field images : 60 images, acquired in groups of 10 during the scan — 10 before projection collection began and 10 after projection collection was completed Artefacts and Imaging Issues - Random bright pixels caused by electron scattering - Ring artefacts, often caused by bright defects on the scintillator - Unknown optical distortion - Possible small tilt of the sample The files for example reconstruction without artefact correction are included (assumed rotation centre at 1866.0; 8-bit output volume)
title: X-ray CT projection dataset of a composite plate with scintillator and distortion artefacts (Diamond Light Source I12, 2009)
