summary: **Background:** Correlations between RNA and protein abundance do not directly specify whether a researcher would select the same tissues from each modality. **Objective:** Compare exploratory top-three tissue sets from restricted mitochondrial relative-pathway RNA scores with protein-abundance comparator sets in the fixed 29-tissue Wang atlas, and identify specified score and membership choices that change that finite comparison. **Methods:** Public processed gene-level measurements were linked to official MitoCarta3.0 terminal memberships. Pathways required at least five uniquely mapped genes with positive, complete measurements in both modalities across all 29 labels. Arithmetic gene means and mean target/reference ratios yielded dimensionless scores. All-gene and nuclear-only panels were evaluated with published abundances and within-gene median scaling. Exact sets, overlap, capture fractions and Jaccard agreement were calculated with an explicit boundary-tie rule; six perturbation families were evaluated separately. An independently coded scalar replay checked all 23,012 scenarios. Pathways and scenarios were not biological replicates; no population tests or sampling intervals were calculated. **Results:** In the published-abundance/all-gene baseline, 8, 29, 16 and 2 of 55 pathways shared zero, one, two and three selected tissues, respectively. Exact recovery occurred for 3 of 55 nuclear-only pathways and 2 of 55 pathways in each median-scaled configuration. In the all-gene published-abundance configuration, replacing the reference aggregation with a geometric reference changed RNA sets for 33 of 55 pathways and protein sets for 38 of 55; excluding individually overlapping references changed each modality for 4 of 55. These are finite, family-specific changes, not uncertainty intervals. **Conclusion:** RNA and protein generally yield different exploratory tissue shortlists under this restricted score. When protein-based relative abundance is the intended atlas-selection target, pathway-specific agreement should be inspected before substituting an RNA shortlist. Protein abundance is a measured comparator, not pathway activity; biological causes, donor-population transfer and prospective tissue-model utility remain untested.

These are finite, family-specific changes, not uncertainty intervals. **Conclusion:** RNA and protein generally yield different exploratory tissue shortlists under this restricted score. When protein-based relative abundance is the intended atlas-selection target, pathway-specific agreement should be inspected before substituting an RNA shortlist. Protein abundance is a measured comparator, not pathway activity; biological causes, donor-population transfer and prospective tissue-model utility remain untested.

summary: The paper studies the critical vanishing-diffusivity limit of a forced, stationary passive-scalar equation inside a laminar, steady, unforced Navier–Stokes flow on the three-torus. For κ > 0 and a friction parameter γ ≥ 0, a smooth scalar source Q is advected, diffused, and damped according to γ g_{κ,γ} + ∂ₓ g_{κ,γ} − κ Δ g_{κ,γ} = Q. summary: This directory contains an index.html file with links to the run directories for Runs A-N of Table 3 and idl plotting routines with secondary data for the 14 figures of the paper "Evolutionary tracks and isochrones of the inverse Hall cascade" by Axel Brandenburg & Vinay Kumar. Each run directory contains the input files (start.in, run.in, print.in, etc), the files src/Makefile.local and src/cparam.local with the relevant compile information, and a data directory with time_series.dat files and data for energy spectra (power_kin.dat, power_lr.dat, powero.dat), and jobid.dat files with code revision numbers and compile times. A readily browsable URL with the same information is available on https://norlx65.nordita.org/~brandenb/projects/Hall-Endpoints/. If anything turns out to be incomplete, or you want data in some other format, please email brandenb@nordita.org.

summary: Features GM-rPIE and GM-MAGPIE reconstruction Added geometric-mean rPIE and multigrid MAGPIE reconstruction through MAGPIEOptions and Reconstructors.MAGPIE . Set reconstructor_options.multigrid_levels = 1 for GM-rPIE or a larger valid depth for GM-MAGPIE. Added joint synthesis of object and shared-probe updates from random minibatches, with native gradient-based position correction and post-epoch constraints. Each additional multigrid level halves both spatial dimensions using 2-by-2 block averaging. The initial implementation supports a single object slice, a single coherent shared probe, matching object/probe/detector sampling, and patch-based object sampling. Both object and probe are updated on every minibatch. Setup validates the supported configuration, multigrid depth, and initial guesses, including the requirement for nonzero amplitude at every object pixel. Full-object sampling for near-field ptychography Added ForwardModelOptions.shift_operator with ShiftOperators.AUTO , PATCH , and FULL_OBJECT . The default AUTO selects full-object sampling when the propagation distance is finite and both probe dimensions strictly exceed 80% of the corresponding object dimensions on the probe pixel grid. Set PATCH to explicitly select patch extraction and placement. Added periodic shifting of complete object slices, followed by a fixed center crop or zero-padding to match the probe shape. Fourier, bilinear, and nearest interpolation are supported, with matching additive adjoints. Features crossing an object boundary wrap to the opposite side. Integrated full-object sampling into AD, BH, DM, LSQML, PIE, and RAAR reconstruction, including object/probe resampling, illumination maps, and position derivatives. Fourier or bilinear interpolation supports gradient-based position refinement; nearest interpolation has zero position derivatives almost everywhere. DM and RAAR use stabilized normalized-adjoint updates for full-object sampling. These are approximate projections for fractional interpolation, so convergence can differ from patch sampling. Bug fixes Corrected the adjoint of image shifting with replicated edge padding and applied the matching padding to analytical probe updates, preserving contributions from boundary pixels. Corrected the object smoothness kernel by placing its central weight at the center of the 3-by-3 stencil. Clarified that smoothing acts on the real and imaginary components of each object slice. Corrected support-based object position origins to use ceil(size / 2) - 0.5 , fixing inconsistent centering for odd object sizes. Fixed a probe-position update crash when clip_update_magnitude_by_mad is disabled and a user-specified update limit is configured. Updated probe rescaling and object-preconditioner initialization to account for the detector propagator's intensity normalization. rescale_probe() and get_probe_renormalization_factor() now accept a propagator argument, retaining the unnormalized far-field Fourier transform as the default. Added ptychi.propagate.get_intensity_scaling_factor() for converting between source- and detector-plane intensity sums under lossless propagation. Added setuptools as an explicit runtime dependency.
title: AdvancedPhotonSource/pty-chi: v2.3.0

summary: Research artifact for the journal article Fresh on Paper, Reused in Code: Static Detection of Hidden Key Reuse in Cancelable Biometric Systems (submitted to the Journal of Information Security and Applications). The archive contains a non-executing Python static analyzer that traces record-dependent key provenance to reviewed BioHash, IoM-GRP and PolyProtect protection calls and reports reuse , conditional_fresh or unknown ; the internally authored source-case benchmarks with expected labels and Bandit outputs; analyzer development and confirmation results (v1-v3, intraprocedural baseline, branch counterexample and regression); experiment protocols and configurations; and aggregate results of the matched key-policy remediation and utility studies. Unit tests and benchmark commands are documented in README.md . Not included: MOBIO, FEI or SCface images, face embeddings, identity-level scores, keys, protected templates or trained model weights. These datasets must be obtained from their custodians under their terms of use.
title: Fresh on Paper, Reused in Code: Static Detection of Hidden Key Reuse in Cancelable Biometric Systems (JISA Artifact)

summary: Reproducible processed-data comparisons accompanying "Training–Test Representation and Reference-Path Sensitivity in a Satellite-Based Maize Gross Primary Production Benchmark". The principal comparison retains 642 site–date observations (489 distinct calendar dates), four maize site-seasons and two regions. A separate retrospective Mead hindcast retains 437 site–date test observations (291 distinct calendar dates); its 480 later-year training observations reuse the principal population. The package retains 120 original B/C model objects, matched cases, dependent nighttime GPP fitting/scoring paths, unchanged validation roles and declared aggregation. The cross-input analysis is a post-review exposed-domain computational diagnosis. It does not establish independent regional or forecasting validation, physical daily-footprint correction, isolated uStar effects or unique causal attribution. The records include the matching Graphical Abstract in compact PNG, vector PDF and larger PNG renditions with its English caption. It illustrates the principal random-forest pipeline and conditional training contrasts, with no new model fit or scientific result. The software includes the deterministic drawing source; font software is excluded and retains its own rights. Supported by Chonnam National University (Grant No. 2026-1417-01) and the Basic Science Research Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (Grant No. NRF-2021R1A2C2004459). Neither funder was involved in design, data collection, analysis or interpretation, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit. CC BY4.0 covers project rights only; upstream provider attribution and other retained notices apply. Original model bytes and scientific values are retained. The companion software provides verified assembly, model replay and current publication-figure reconstruction. Graphical Abstract content and caption are CC BY4.0; the drawing source is MIT. Embedded font rights remain with the font owner; font software is not redistributed. Code repository: https://github.com/jonghanko/maize-gpp-reference-spatial-support .
title: Training–Test Representation and Reference-Path Sensitivity in a Satellite-Based Maize Gross Primary Production Benchmark — processed data, model artifacts and results

summary: This replication package accompanies the manuscript  “How much coverage is enough? Spatially balanced partial-coverage thermal drone surveys for estimating ungulate density in forested landscapes.” The archive contains the R and Python code, georeferenced full-survey detections, observed partial-survey data, retrospective transect-intersection inputs, survey geometries, terrain inputs, compact simulation outputs and verification results needed to reproduce the drone-survey analyses. It includes workflows for reconstructing the reported full- and partial-coverage density estimates, statistical comparisons, perturbation analyses and post-processing simulation experiments. The original bootstrap analysis used 999 resamples without a recorded random seed. The archived workflow fixes the seed at 42; consequently, some bootstrap confidence limits and downstream test statistics differ slightly through Monte Carlo variation, while the reported conclusions remain unchanged. These differences are documented explicitly in the package. Raw survey videos, MOT annotation archives, raw camera-trap images and event-level camera-trap data are not redistributed. The archive instead contains the derived georeferenced detections and available transect-level inputs used by the reported drone analyses, which are actually required for replicating the results. The camera-trap comparison is represented by the area-level summary values used in the manuscript. Additional exclusions and their justification are documented in  docs/EXCLUSIONS.md . Reproduction instructions, a data dictionary, provenance information, validation results, software-environment details and a file-level checksum manifest are included.
title: Replication Package: How much coverage is enough? Spatially balanced partial-coverage thermal drone surveys for estimating ungulate density in forested landscapes

summary: Software engineering agents resend their entire trajectory to an LLM at every turn, motivating online trajectory reduction. Prior work shows that randomly deleting 75% of tokens in old turns may preserve agent effectiveness, but it remains unclear why, how agents compensate for missing content, and whether it actually reduces costs. This paper presents an empirical study of 42 trajectory-reduction configurations, focusing on effectiveness, agent behavior, and cost. We systematically explore deleting content from old turns by varying the scope, granularity, amount, and timing of deletion across 9,400 runs with two state-of-the-art agents on SWE-bench Verified. We find deleting large amounts of trajectory content (e.g., up to 100% of reasoning text) can preserve overall effectiveness. Importantly, such deletion must be applied with a delay, as immediate deletion tends to significantly degrade effectiveness. Agents often compensate for deleted content by re-fetching it, increasing both the number of turns taken and the input/output tokens. Whether trajectory reduction reduces costs depends on the pricing model: Under a flat pricing model, estimated costs fall in 26 of 42 evaluations. Surprisingly, under a caching-aware pricing model, zero evaluations yield lower costs, since reducing the trajectory breaks the cached prefix billed at a lower rate. Our findings have three implications: First, token counts alone are misleading; trajectory reduction techniques must consider overall costs under a realistic pricing model. Second, analyzing trajectories is crucial to understand agent behavior, as end-to-end effectiveness hides differences such as excessive re-fetching. Finally, these results highlight the need for future work on memory management to reduce costs without sacrificing effectiveness.
title: The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents

summary: The proliferation of orbital sensing data and the real-time demands of emerging global services are pushing low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks from bent-pipe relays toward intelligent onboard processing. This shift confronts a fundamental tension, where modern artificial intelligence (AI) training paradigms require intensive computation, abundant memory, and stable connectivity, all of which are scarce under the dynamic topologies, intermittent links, and severe size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints of satellite networks. Addressing this tension demands rethinking AI workflows, from training and inference to the emerging deployment of large language models (LLMs), under a constraint-aware design philosophy. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first survey that jointly covers all three, whereas prior surveys examine these aspects in isolation. We begin by identifying the deployment challenge of satellite intelligence (SI) and deriving design principles for SI. We then examine three advancing paradigms: i) distributed training, where federated learning (FL) and split learning (SL) enable satellite-ground co-training under resource limitations; ii) collaborative inference, which exploits single-satellite, multi-satellite, and satellite-ground architectures to meet real-time service demands; and iii) on-orbit LLM adaptation and serving, which tackles the frontier challenge of deploying LLMs under severe orbital constraints and resource-aware serving. Finally, we identify open challenges and future directions. By bridging the AI and satellite networks, this paper provides a research roadmap for the implementation of space-native AI technologies.
title: Satellite Intelligence: Distributed Training, Collaborative Inference,and LLM Adaptation in LEO Constellation

summary: Multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning (MOMARL) addresses agent coordination and objective trade-offs simultaneously while optimising overall system performance. Existing work tends to treat multi-agent cooperation and multi-objective optimisation as largely independent components of a learning problem, which amounts to an exorbitant complexity except in trivial cases. We study here whether the structure provided by multiple objectives can itself be exploited to facilitate cooperation, rather than being treated as an additional optimisation challenge. We formulate MOMARL at both the team and individual levels and introduce objective-wise counterfactual credit assignment to evaluate each agent's contribution across the team objectives. We propose Meta-Gradient Informed Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MIRL), with static (MIRL-S) and dynamic (MIRL-D) variants. By incorporating meta-gradient information, MIRL enables agents to learn how to prioritise objectives individually while collectively optimising the system-level objective, allowing the multi-objective structure to directly guide cooperation. Experiments on a multi-objective multiple particle environment show that our methods improve Pareto-front quality over baselines, with the dynamic variant achieving the strongest performance.
title: Preference-Guided Cooperation in Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

summary: Disease diagnosis is a key application of large language model (LLM) agents in healthcare. However, existing medical agents are primarily trained and evaluated with static question-answering data, providing limited opportunities to learn active information acquisition, examination decision-making, and dynamic clinical interaction. To address this limitation, we present ClinVerse, an interactive, real-data-grounded multi-agent environment designed for training and evaluating medical diagnostic agents. Built on ClinPatient, a scalable dataset comprising 150k diagnostic cases derived from real-world electronic health records, ClinVerse supports coordinated interactions among six specialized clinical roles. Specifically, a doctor agent starts from an initial patient complaint, progressively gathers clinical evidence through patient interviews and examination requests, and ultimately produces a diagnosis. For each interaction trajectory, a rule-based scoring framework quantifies information acquisition, examination ordering, and diagnostic accuracy. These trajectory-level scores serve as reward signals for agent training while also enabling scalable evaluation. In experiments, we evaluate various general-purpose and medical-domain models and show that nine self-evolution methods across three categories consistently improve agents' diagnostic capabilities within ClinVerse. We further analyze the interplay among model capability, environment feedback, and self-evolution methods.
title: ClinVerse: A Realistic Multi-Agent Diagnostic Environment for Training and Evaluating Medical Agents

summary: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) has become the dominant paradigm in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), motivating extensive study of what privileged information should be made available to the critic during training. While prior work has examined the role of global state in fully cooperative settings, the design of centralized critics for N-agent ad hoc teamwork - in which dynamically varying set of learning agents must coordinate with an arbitrary set of uncontrolled teammates drawn from an unknown distribution - remains poorly understood. We study this question by comparing two natural classes of advantage estimators: controlled history estimators, which condition only on the observation and action histories of the learner's own agents, and joint history estimators, which additionally condition on the histories of the uncontrolled teammates. We prove that both estimators are unbiased and characterize the conditions under which the joint history estimate attains strictly lower variance than its controlled counterpart. Empirically, joint history critics match or outperform controlled history critics across a range of NAHT tasks, yielding improved sample efficiency and final returns. Together, these results provide both a theoretical justification and an empirical recommendation for incorporating uncontrolled agent histories into centralized critics for N-agent ad hoc teamwork.
title: Centralized Critics for N-Agent Ad Hoc Teamwork

summary: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.
title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning supports cooperative decision-making in Internet of Things systems, but strategic deviations can disrupt coordination and undermine confidence in the training process. This paper proposes Blockchain-Enabled Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (BE-CTDE), which uses blockchain as an active training-management layer. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations; its flags drive a token mechanism combining slashing, burning, rewards, and compensation. Retained balances determine each agent's contribution to the global policy update, connecting auditable behavior to learning influence. We derive a one-round incentive condition that accounts for action-dependent compensation and the payoff from deviation, and a finite expected exclusion-time bound under explicit conditional detection and accounting assumptions, showing perfect detection is unnecessary. An exact finite-population capacity bound characterizes the limits of the population-relative detector. In multi-agent path finding experiments, BE-CTDE outperforms a state-of-the-art learning-based path planner with substantially higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries form the majority. It also outperforms partially defended baselines in all configurations, with collision rates up to 35% lower than under detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than under conventional stake slashing. Together, these results characterize how behavioral verification and token feedback can support accountable cooperative learning.
title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics

summary: In large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, reported confidence increasingly determines the allocation of scarce downstream attention, computation, and decision influence. This makes reporting strategic: an agent may overstate the relevance of its contribution even when its underlying belief is well calibrated. Existing calibration methods largely assume passive reporting and therefore do not address strategic incentives created when confidence determines downstream allocation. We formulate strategic calibration as a reporting-layer incentive problem and propose the Audited Pivot Scoring Mechanism (APSM). APSM offsets platform-controlled allocation benefits, uses inverse-propensity-weighted sparse audits, charges the Clarke pivot externality, and applies a strictly proper score. Under the stated model assumptions, truthful reporting is the unique expected-utility best response. We also characterize approximate execution and the audit-variance trade-off. Calculator-free experiments show that LLM agents inflate confidence under Top-$K$ incentives. With a shared agent-local utility interface, LLM agents reduce distortion under both Compensated Proper Scoring (CPS) and APSM. CPS achieves higher exact allocation match, whereas APSM yields lower Brier loss and numerically fewer cutoff crossings. Experiments further show that APSM enlarges the utility margin against allocation-changing deviations by $1.93\times$ and improves robustness under approximate execution. These results support incentive-aware elicitation as a distinct layer for reliable multi-agent coordination.
title: Strategic Calibration in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Audited Pivot Scoring for Truthful Elicitation

summary: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.
title: HA-DiPO: Diffusion Policy Optimization for Heterogeneous Cooperative Transport

summary: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.
title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.
title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Companion data deposit for the manuscript "Data coherence over data volume drives generalisable genome-based prediction of microbial carbon utilisation". This record contains the phenotype labels, genome feature matrices, train/test splits, trained model checkpoints, predicted proteomes, and figure and table source data underlying every script-generated display item in the manuscript and its supplementary material. The code that consumes it is on GitHub (links below); this record contains data only. CONTENTS - trait-prediction-data.zip (60 MB, 453 MB unpacked). All derived data: KOFAM, RAST and GapMind feature matrices, harmonised phenotype tables, train/test splits for the random, leave-one-dataset-out and phylogeny-based evaluations, the pruned GTDB tree and distance matrix, KEGG reference mappings, source data for every script-generated main-text and supplementary figure and table, and 105 trained CatBoost checkpoints. Unpacks to a data/ tree that mirrors the analysis repository. - proteomes_all_seqs.zip (766 MB, 1.5 GB unpacked). 829 predicted-protein FASTA files: one for each of the 822 selected genome records, the input to the KOFAM and GapMind annotation, plus seven alternate assemblies of Marine strains included in the pangenome-completeness analysis. - Per-dataset phenotype matrices and genome tables, provided loose so they can be read without downloading an archive: atleaf (206 genomes x 44 substrates), biolog (362 x 59), marine (172 x 100, with 199 genome records in the genome table) and populus (55 x 175, plus a no-carbon control column). - genome_accessions.tsv, mapping all 822 genome records to NCBI, BV-BRC or JGI IMG accessions, with public KBase download links for the 166 Cedar Creek (CCESR) Biolog genomes. - biolog_assay_provenance.tsv, recording for each of the 362 Biolog genomes the assay type (Biolog plate or other assay), the originating source (source-study PMIDs for 193; the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection for 166; unpublished contributions for 2; not recorded for 1) and how the genome is paired with its phenotype record, since that dataset is a compilation rather than a single assay campaign. - substrate_identity_common15.csv and substrate_identity_all.csv, binding every phenotype column to the exact compound the originating study assayed. 46 Biolog and Populus columns, including all 30 in the 15 shared phenotypes, also carry a Biolog PM1/PM2A well position that identifies the compound (for the Biolog compilation, a compound reference rather than the well each source study used). - Populus_carbon_source_results.xlsx, the ORNL Plant-Microbe Interfaces Biolog assay as measured by Leah Hochanadel and Dale A. Pelletier, released publicly for the first time with this work and separately deposited at ORNL/OSTI doi:10.25983/PMI/3399550. - README.md with the full file-by-file description, dataset provenance, and reproduction instructions. MD5SUMS.txt for verification. SCOPE Four carbon-source utilisation datasets were harmonised: ATLeaf (Arabidopsis thaliana leaf isolates), Biolog (a compilation of published studies, the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection and unpublished contributions), Marine (heterotrophic marine bacteria) and Populus (Populus deltoides root isolates). Analyses focus on the 15 carbon sources shared by all four, drawn from 240 carbon sources in total. Each carbon source column is bound to a single compound, so distinct isomers are never merged. REUSE The deployment checkpoints in data/outputs/full_data_models/ and data/outputs/concordant_full_models/ give one CatBoost model per phenotype, trained on all labelled genomes and on the GapMind-concordant subset respectively. Each ships with metadata, feature importances and its selected-feature list, so a phenotype can be predicted for a new genome from its KOFAM presence/absence vector without retraining. The complete KOFAM, RAST and GapMind annotation matrices are also included for reuse. SOURCES AND CITATION Phenotype data originate w

summary: A cube can pass through a straight tunnel cut through another cube of the same size. From this seventeenth-century geometric paradox to recent counterexamples to the  Rupert property, the problem has developed into a broader question concerning projections of convex bodies. The first part of this article reviews the historical background and introduces the essential geometric tools, including a vector-based reconstruction of the classical cube-passage configuration. The second part studies centred convex bodies whose support functions are expressed as spherical harmonic perturbations of the support function of a ball. For these bodies, we establish an exact passage  criterion, construct explicit positive certificates for passage, and classify the three-parameter family \[T_{a,b,c}=aP_4(x)+bP_4(y)+cP_4(z) : \] the equality $D_2(T_{a,b,c}) = 0$ holds if and only if $ab = ac = bc = 0$. Proofs are included throughout.
title: Prince Rupert's Problem: Geometric Foundations, Historical Background, and New Results on Convex Bodies

summary: Supplementary data for "OpenScientist: evaluating an open agentic AI co-scientist to accelerate biomedical discovery." This dataset contains research logs, knowledge states, provenance files, and generated figures for seven case studies spanning neurodegenerative disease transcriptomics, multiple myeloma genomics, survival proteomics, drug side effect analysis, and more. Each case study includes the full agent iteration log, configuration, and final report. Input datasets are included for three case studies where data sharing is permitted: case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics), case study 4 (multiple myeloma RNA-seq), and case study 7 (drug side effect frequencies from clinical trials).  Version 2 (August 2026) adds supplementary material for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics): 60 additional independent runs of the same question and dataset, comparing three agent/model configurations — Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8, and the omp harness with Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 — each run 10 times online and 10 times in a fully air-gapped configuration with no network access and literature served from a local 40-million-article MEDLINE mirror. Files: ..._supplemental_online_30runs_data.tar.gz and ..._supplemental_airgapped_30runs_data.tar.gz each contain 30 runs with reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), all generated figures, per-iteration transcripts, the exact prompt, and full version/commit provenance. ..._supplemental_60runs_metrics.csv gives per-run runtime, tool-call counts, literature searches, findings recorded and token usage for all 60 runs. Version 3 (September 2026) adds two further supplementary sets for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics). ..._supplemental_reproducibility_10runs_data.tar.gz contains 10 independent runs of the same question on Claude Opus 4.6, all run on 2026-03-08 with byte-identical inputs (the research question and the input .h5ad were SHA-256 verified identical across all 10) and a 10-iteration budget. Each run includes the report (Markdown, PDF, HTML), knowledge_state.json with structured findings and literature list, per-iteration transcripts, and the job UUID. These runs quantify run-to-run variability under fixed inputs. ..._supplemental_genomic_skill_comparison_data.tar.gz contains 30 runs — 15 using the original genomics Agent Skill and 15 using a revised version — with the two skill definitions included alongside the jobs. The revised skill adds explicit guidance on donor-level pseudobulk aggregation and mixed-effect modelling; the paired arms allow the effect of that guidance on the analysis the agent chooses to be assessed directly. Each run includes reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), per-iteration provenance transcripts, and container logs. summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). The pooled robustness estimate (Δ = 0.25 → 0.46; d = 0.68; the primary main-wave cohort gives Δ = 0.24 → 0.45, d = 0.67) rests on that single item and, in an exploratory country split, on the UK sample, and it falls to d = 0.09 once the item is removed. A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. summary: la versione 5  documenta riprende la versione 1 e la versione 3 e la versione 4  chiude il ciclo aperto dalla V4 e ne sostituisce integralmente i risultati numerici. Il documento riporta cinque punti fisici verificati sul modello a 240 nm (P1–P5), uno studio sistematico della scala da 1 nm a 1 m (S1–S4), la caratteriz zazione in microgravità e per tre classi di materiale (SP1–SP5), la simulazione dei fluidi con i due rotori come ostacoli (F1–F2) e il regime di vuoto profondo con assenza di attrito (V1–V5). La coppia ottica è trattata con un solo modello, il momento angolare ceduto dal fascio: τ = Pass/ωott = Fλ/2π = 2.610×10−24 N·m, cioè 108volte menodellimiteafasciointero P/ωott = 2.824×10−22 N·m, che coincide con la τmax dichiarata nella V4 (2.826×10−22). Poiché Per = τ/kT, il criterio di determinismo si riduce a un rapporto di potenze: Per = Pass/15.16 µW. Con 1 µW e l’intercettazione reale dello 0.924 % si ottiene 6.10×10−4 a 240 nm, 1.93×10−14 a 1 nm e 6.60×10−2 a 1 m: il dispositivo è termicamente limitato a ogni scala, e la soglia Per = 1 richiede 1.64 mW. A 1 GHz la configurazione in rameè strutturalmente impossibile(limite 72.6MHz). Nelvuotoprofondononesisteregimestazionario: esisteuntempocritico di rottura, che la scala governa (30.53 s a 240 nm, 2.538×1024 s a 1 m, un fattore 8.3×1022), mentre il materiale governa la velocità di rottura (31.909) e l’energia immagazzinata (250). Nessuna validazione sperimentale è rivendicata: ogni cifra è prodotta dagli script in Appendice A. Document version 5 build s upon versions 1, 3, and 4; it concludes the cycle initiated by version 4 and entirely replaces its numerical results. The document presents: five physical points verified on the 240 nm model (P1–P5); a systematic study across scales ranging from 1 nm to 1 m (S1–S4); characterization in microgravity for three classes of materials (SP1–SP5); fluid simulations with the two rotors acting as obstacles (F1–F2); and the deep-vacuum regime in the absence of friction (V1–V5). Optical torque is addressed using a single model—the angular momentum transferred by the beam: τ = Pass/ωott = Fλ/2π = 2.610×10⁻²⁴ N·m. This value is 10⁸ times smaller than the limit for a full beam (P/ωott = 2.824×10⁻²² N·m), which aligns with the τmax stated in version 4 (2.826×10⁻²²). Since Per = τ/kT, the criterion for determinism simplifies to a ratio of powers: Per = Pass/15.16 µW. With an input of 1 µW and an actual interception rate of 0.924%, the resulting values are 6.10×10⁻⁴ at 240 nm, 1.93×10⁻¹⁴ at 1 nm, and 6.60×10⁻² at 1 m. The device is thus thermally limited at every scale, and reaching the threshold of Per = 1 requires 1.64 mW. At 1 GHz, the copper-based configuration is structurally impossible (the limit is 72.6 MHz). In a high vacuum, no steady state exists; instead, there is a critical time to failure, which is governed by the scale (30.53 s at 240 nm, 2.538×10²⁴ s at 1 m—a factor of 8.3×10²²), while the material determines the rate of failure (31.909) and the stored energy (250). No experimental validation is claimed: every figure is generated by the scripts in Appendix A.

summary: Supplementary material for the paper "Business-Rule Admissibility in Process-Based Business Simulation" (Yan Fang, University of Southern California). It holds what is needed to check and reproduce the paper's results without the simulation framework: the study firm's handbook and the model's prose; the rule sets R (104 rules) and R0 (82 rules), each rule with the passage it formalises and its SQL query; the specification of every re-injected defect; the protocols of the pre-registered replication, the control rule set, the further mutants and the robust indicator score, with the hashes they froze; the instructions given to each agent and path-level records of each agent's file access; the scripts that apply the rules and compute the indicators, event-log distances and tables; and the databases and change histories of all 430 simulation runs. The simulation framework (NAILU) and the model's intermediate representation are proprietary to Aurite AI and are not included. Files: README.md (contents, and how to reproduce the tables), SHA256SUMS (the hash of every file), materials.zip, and three archives of runs (exploratory seeds 1–10; confirmatory seeds 11–30; further mutants, seeds 11–30). Unzip all archives into one folder next to README.md and SHA256SUMS; sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS then verifies the package.

summary: This paper resolves the foundational deadlock of classical General Relativity metric engineering—namely, the requirement for unphysical, stellar-scale quantities of negative energy in models such as the Alcubierre warp drive. The bottleneck is shown to stem directly from the standard treatment of spacetime as an incompressible, geometrically rigid continuum. By reformulating the problem within Quantum Modified General Relativity (QMOGER) and Gordon’s optical metric, the vacuum is modeled as an active, compressible, barotropic superfluid. Consequently, the energy threshold required for propulsive metric modulation is governed by the polarizability of the quantum electrodynamic (QED) electron-positron vacuum rather than Planck-scale geometric stiffness, reducing the required energy barrier by more than twenty orders of magnitude. Key Mechanisms: Pressure-Driven Dynamic Casimir Effect: Rather than introducing exotic negative mass, the system leverages relativistic optical phase modulation driven by ultra-short laser bursts. Non-adiabatic boundary modulation converts virtual vacuum fluctuations into real photons, generating multi-megabar non-equilibrium radiation pressure spikes and steep spatial gradients while keeping total integrated pulse energy minimal. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) Structural Stabilization: To prevent three-dimensional turbulent enstrophy cascades from tearing the metric envelope apart, an external toroidal magnetic field is applied. At high interaction parameters, field-parallel velocity gradients are extinguished by anisotropic Joule dissipation, collapsing the flow into a quasi-two-dimensional regime. This eliminates vortex stretching and triggers an inverse energy cascade, causing microscopic injected energy to naturally self-organize into a stable, macroscopic warp envelope. Nonlinear QED Dielectric Phase Transition: Incorporating the Heisenberg–Euler effective Lagrangian under high magnetic fields, the vacuum exhibits intensity-dependent birefringence. At a critical relative intensity threshold, the vacuum undergoes a sharp dielectric phase transition that initiates direct macroscopic momentum coupling between the electromagnetic field and the vacuum substrate. Conclusion & Experimental Relevance: The manuscript replaces astronomical negative-mass speculation with concrete non-equilibrium quantum optical and magnetohydrodynamic processes. It provides closed tensor field equations, complete dimensional consistency, and a realistic experimental roadmap testable at high-intensity petawatt laser and high-field superconducting magnet facilities.

summary: LaTeX source, figures, check program and Lean 4 file of the paper Weak-Type Endpoint Bounds for Bochner-Riesz Means in Every Dimension by Deep Bhattacharjee. At the critical index lambda(p) = n(1/p - 1/2) - 1/2, the Bochner-Riesz means (1 - |xi|^a/t^a)^lambda_+ in every dimension n >= 2 map L^p to weak L^p for 1 < p < 2n/(n+1), uniformly in t, and converge in weak L^p (Theorem A); they have (p,q) sparse bounds for (n-1)p/(n+1-2p) < q < p', which is sharp on the critical side of the trapezoid of Beltran, Roos and Seeger except at its corner (Theorem B); and they map L^p(w) to weak L^p(w) for every A_1 weight w in RH_sigma when 1 < p < 1 + (n-1)/(n+1)(1 - 1/sigma) (Theorem C), a range that by the self-improvement of reverse Hoelder inequalities includes its right end point. For n >= 3 these follow from OpenAI's preprint 'Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation' (25 October 2026), which proves the local smoothing and Bochner-Riesz conjectures, through the conditional theorems of Tao and of Beltran, Roos and Seeger. The paper reproduces OpenAI's argument and the epsilon-removal of Beltran, Roos and Seeger in full, with credit, and then applies their sparse domination theorem and the weighted theorem of Frey and Nieraeth. The Python program checks the algebraic identities and exponent computations; the Lean file proves the exponent arithmetic and the quaternion identities. No statement of the paper depends on them.
title: Source and verification code for the paper Weak-Type Endpoint Bounds for Bochner-Riesz Means in Every Dimension

For n >= 3 these follow from OpenAI's preprint 'Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation' (25 October 2026), which proves the local smoothing and Bochner-Riesz conjectures, through the conditional theorems of Tao and of Beltran, Roos and Seeger. The paper reproduces OpenAI's argument and the epsilon-removal of Beltran, Roos and Seeger in full, with credit, and then applies their sparse domination theorem and the weighted theorem of Frey and Nieraeth. The Python program checks the algebraic identities and exponent computations; the Lean file proves the exponent arithmetic and the quaternion identities. No statement of the paper depends on them.

summary: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.
title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

summary: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs. We present Private Authentication for Rotational Secrecy (PARS), a reference mechanism that coordinates policy-triggered key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among authorized Physical AI agents. For deployments that need distributed agreement on security state, we further develop the PARS-Enabled Edge Security Ledger (PARS-ESL), an optional permissioned architecture maintained by authorized validators or capable edge gateways. PARS-ESL does not store high-volume operational transactions. Instead, it records authenticated state for key epochs, group membership, revocation, algorithm-suite policies, challenge validation, and recovery checkpoints. As a result, resource-constrained agents can take part as lightweight clients, and low-latency operational traffic stays outside the ledger consensus path, protected by the currently active symmetric epoch keys. Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.
title: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents

summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.
title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Companion data deposit for the manuscript "Data coherence over data volume drives generalisable genome-based prediction of microbial carbon utilisation". This record contains the phenotype labels, genome feature matrices, train/test splits, trained model checkpoints, predicted proteomes, and figure and table source data underlying every script-generated display item in the manuscript and its supplementary material. The code that consumes it is on GitHub (links below); this record contains data only. CONTENTS - trait-prediction-data.zip (60 MB, 453 MB unpacked). All derived data: KOFAM, RAST and GapMind feature matrices, harmonised phenotype tables, train/test splits for the random, leave-one-dataset-out and phylogeny-based evaluations, the pruned GTDB tree and distance matrix, KEGG reference mappings, source data for every script-generated main-text and supplementary figure and table, and 105 trained CatBoost checkpoints. Unpacks to a data/ tree that mirrors the analysis repository. - proteomes_all_seqs.zip (766 MB, 1.5 GB unpacked). 829 predicted-protein FASTA files: one for each of the 822 selected genome records, the input to the KOFAM and GapMind annotation, plus seven alternate assemblies of Marine strains included in the pangenome-completeness analysis. - Per-dataset phenotype matrices and genome tables, provided loose so they can be read without downloading an archive: atleaf (206 genomes x 44 substrates), biolog (362 x 59), marine (172 x 100, with 199 genome records in the genome table) and populus (55 x 175, plus a no-carbon control column). - genome_accessions.tsv, mapping all 822 genome records to NCBI, BV-BRC or JGI IMG accessions, with public KBase download links for the 166 Cedar Creek (CCESR) Biolog genomes. - biolog_assay_provenance.tsv, recording for each of the 362 Biolog genomes the assay type (Biolog plate or other assay), the originating source (source-study PMIDs for 193; the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection for 166; unpublished contributions for 2; not recorded for 1) and how the genome is paired with its phenotype record, since that dataset is a compilation rather than a single assay campaign. - substrate_identity_common15.csv and substrate_identity_all.csv, binding every phenotype column to the exact compound the originating study assayed. 46 Biolog and Populus columns, including all 30 in the 15 shared phenotypes, also carry a Biolog PM1/PM2A well position that identifies the compound (for the Biolog compilation, a compound reference rather than the well each source study used). - Populus_carbon_source_results.xlsx, the ORNL Plant-Microbe Interfaces Biolog assay as measured by Leah Hochanadel and Dale A. Pelletier, released publicly for the first time with this work and separately deposited at ORNL/OSTI doi:10.25983/PMI/3399550. - README.md with the full file-by-file description, dataset provenance, and reproduction instructions. MD5SUMS.txt for verification. SCOPE Four carbon-source utilisation datasets were harmonised: ATLeaf (Arabidopsis thaliana leaf isolates), Biolog (a compilation of published studies, the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection and unpublished contributions), Marine (heterotrophic marine bacteria) and Populus (Populus deltoides root isolates). Analyses focus on the 15 carbon sources shared by all four, drawn from 240 carbon sources in total. Each carbon source column is bound to a single compound, so distinct isomers are never merged. REUSE The deployment checkpoints in data/outputs/full_data_models/ and data/outputs/concordant_full_models/ give one CatBoost model per phenotype, trained on all labelled genomes and on the GapMind-concordant subset respectively. Each ships with metadata, feature importances and its selected-feature list, so a phenotype can be predicted for a new genome from its KOFAM presence/absence vector without retraining. The complete KOFAM, RAST and GapMind annotation matrices are also included for reuse. SOURCES AND CITATION Phenotype data originate w

summary: Supplementary data for "OpenScientist: evaluating an open agentic AI co-scientist to accelerate biomedical discovery." This dataset contains research logs, knowledge states, provenance files, and generated figures for seven case studies spanning neurodegenerative disease transcriptomics, multiple myeloma genomics, survival proteomics, drug side effect analysis, and more. Each case study includes the full agent iteration log, configuration, and final report. Input datasets are included for three case studies where data sharing is permitted: case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics), case study 4 (multiple myeloma RNA-seq), and case study 7 (drug side effect frequencies from clinical trials).  Version 2 (August 2026) adds supplementary material for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics): 60 additional independent runs of the same question and dataset, comparing three agent/model configurations — Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8, and the omp harness with Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 — each run 10 times online and 10 times in a fully air-gapped configuration with no network access and literature served from a local 40-million-article MEDLINE mirror. Files: ..._supplemental_online_30runs_data.tar.gz and ..._supplemental_airgapped_30runs_data.tar.gz each contain 30 runs with reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), all generated figures, per-iteration transcripts, the exact prompt, and full version/commit provenance. ..._supplemental_60runs_metrics.csv gives per-run runtime, tool-call counts, literature searches, findings recorded and token usage for all 60 runs. Version 3 (September 2026) adds two further supplementary sets for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics). ..._supplemental_reproducibility_10runs_data.tar.gz contains 10 independent runs of the same question on Claude Opus 4.6, all run on 2026-03-08 with byte-identical inputs (the research question and the input .h5ad were SHA-256 verified identical across all 10) and a 10-iteration budget. Each run includes the report (Markdown, PDF, HTML), knowledge_state.json with structured findings and literature list, per-iteration transcripts, and the job UUID. These runs quantify run-to-run variability under fixed inputs. ..._supplemental_genomic_skill_comparison_data.tar.gz contains 30 runs — 15 using the original genomics Agent Skill and 15 using a revised version — with the two skill definitions included alongside the jobs. The revised skill adds explicit guidance on donor-level pseudobulk aggregation and mixed-effect modelling; the paired arms allow the effect of that guidance on the analysis the agent chooses to be assessed directly. Each run includes reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), per-iteration provenance transcripts, and container logs. Version 4 (October 2026) adds the run sets generated for the second revision of the manuscript, renumbers the case-study files to match the revised manuscript (the suvorexant proteomics analysis is now Case Study 5; neurofibromatosis is Case Study 6, drug side effects Case Study 7, and the CSF Aβ42/40 prediction model Case Study 8), and adds RUNS_MANIFEST.csv , which maps every job in this record to its experiment, supplementary table and row label. Run IDs quoted in the supplementary tables are the first 8 hexadecimal characters of the job ID. New archives, all for Case Study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics; same research question and input file as the existing archives, OpenScientist commit fac6971, Claude Opus 4.6, run 2026-10-18 with a 10-iteration budget): ..._supplemental_iteration_controls_10runs_data.tar.gz (10 replicate runs on unmodified code; Experiment 4 and the control arm of the two ablations), ..._supplemental_knowledge_state_ablation_10runs_data.tar.gz (10 runs in which the knowledge-state summary and outline were withheld from the agent; Experiment 5; the patched orchestrator file is included as ..._knowledge_state_ablation_iteration.py.patched ), and ..._supp

summary: This record holds the data and analysis code underlying the manuscript “Temperature Response of Intrinsic Viscosity in Methacrylate and Hydrocarbon Viscosity Modifiers: A Harmonized Analysis of Published Data” (submitted for publication). The manuscript is not included here. The deposit contains: (1) Supplementary_Dataset_S1.xlsx, the harmonized evidence workbook of 32 worksheets, holding the source registry, the lineage audit, the intrinsic-viscosity observations with chemistry and architecture codes and molecular-weight provenance flags, the per-system temperature slopes, the direct-compatibility records with multiplicity weights, the chemistry-by-architecture coding table, the wax-window analysis, and all model outputs, with source-level provenance on every quantitative record; (2) Supplementary_Dataset_S2_Figure_Data.xlsx, giving the input and plotted values for every figure; (3) Supplementary_Software_S1.zip, the complete Python analysis pipeline with README.md, requirements.txt and MANIFEST.txt, which reads only the two workbooks and regenerates every reported table and figure; and (4) README.md and LICENSE.txt for the record. To reproduce: download all files into one folder, unzip Supplementary_Software_S1.zip, install the packages listed in requirements.txt, and run the following command from inside the Supplementary_Software_S1 folder: python reproduce_all.py --data ../Supplementary_Dataset_S1.xlsx --figdata ../Supplementary_Dataset_S2_Figure_Data.xlsx --out results The pipeline regenerates the one-stage mixed-effects model with publication and system random effects (methacrylate-minus-ethylene-propylene temperature interaction of +0.646 ln units per 100 °C, 95% CI 0.433 to 0.858), the system-slope regressions with wild cluster bootstrap inference (+0.775, p = 0.005), the wax cut-off sensitivity scan, the multiplicity-weighted cross-study compatibility model with chance-level comparisons, the domain-restricted ordinal phase model, and Figures 1–5 and S1. All resampling uses seed 20260918. A full run takes about one hour; adding --bootstrap 500 --reml-bootstrap 49 gives a fast check with identical point estimates. The study is a secondary analysis of published data; no new experiments were performed. Values in the exact-value core were taken from tables or explicit numerical statements in the cited sources, and figure-derived values are excluded from that core. Architecture is recorded as reported by the source authors and is not a measured quantity. summary: Supplementary material for the paper "Business-Rule Admissibility in Process-Based Business Simulation" (Yan Fang, University of Southern California). It holds what is needed to check and reproduce the paper's results without the simulation framework: the study firm's handbook and the model's prose; the rule sets R (104 rules) and R0 (82 rules), each rule with the passage it formalises and its SQL query; the specification of every re-injected defect; the protocols of the pre-registered replication, the control rule set, the further mutants and the robust indicator score, with the hashes they froze; the instructions given to each agent and path-level records of each agent's file access; the scripts that apply the rules and compute the indicators, event-log distances and tables; and the databases and change histories of all 430 simulation runs. The simulation framework (NAILU) and the model's intermediate representation are proprietary to Aurite AI and are not included. Files: README.md (contents, and how to reproduce the tables), SHA256SUMS (the hash of every file), materials.zip, and three archives of runs (exploratory seeds 1–10; confirmatory seeds 11–30; further mutants, seeds 11–30). Unzip all archives into one folder next to README.md and SHA256SUMS; sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS then verifies the package.

summary: Early-warning models in learning analytics can identify learners at risk of failure or withdrawal, but the resulting alerts are often only weakly connected to inspectable learning evidence. A risk score may indicate that intervention is needed without showing which traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the alert. This paper introduces an incremental Learner Digital Twin for evidence-grounded early warning, implemented as a lightweight knowledge graph. The twin is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying learning traces and assessment records, and it serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as an explanation-grounding substrate. Predictive features are derived through graph-mediated queries, while features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records are represented as queryable graph entities. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol. The results show that graph-mediated feature extraction preserves the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints. Generated alerts are materialized as evidence chains linking risk decisions to feature attributions, evidence items, and raw platform records. The study shows that early-warning prediction can be routed through a semantic and provenance-aware representation while preserving predictive performance and adding traceability, verifiability, and evidence-grounded explanation.

summary: Security pipelines often fuse several data sources and protect a downstream model with a cross-source anomaly detector. Such detectors are usually judged by their clean false-positive rate and by how well they catch random corruption. Neither metric captures an adversary who controls some sources and targets a specific downstream decision. We propose a threat-quantification score, the \emph{task-conditioned visibility margin}, defined as the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task. The margin has a closed form, takes about $85\,μ$s per certificate, yields a minimum-evidence attack, and identifies task-relevant directions the detector cannot see. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector that flags 82.8\% of random single-channel corruptions is first-order blind on 64.7\% of task/subset pairs in an audit of one- to four-channel subsets. Task-conditioned manipulations cause more than twice as many falsely reassuring errors as generic stealthy ones, and more of them evade the alarm on four of five splits, mainly at small budgets. Used to prioritize audits on held-out subsets, the margin finds a median of four verified failures in ten checks, compared with none for random order and two for alarm-based ranking, and performs comparably to the task-gradient baseline. It also ranks vulnerable configurations of the learned GDN and TranAD detectors and of a five-source crop-yield panel.
title: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors

summary: Security pipelines often fuse several data sources and protect a downstream model with a cross-source anomaly detector. Such detectors are usually judged by their clean false-positive rate and by how well they catch random corruption. Neither metric captures an adversary who controls some sources and targets a specific downstream decision. We propose a threat-quantification score, the \emph{task-conditioned visibility margin}, defined as the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task. The margin has a closed form, takes about $85\,μ$s per certificate, yields a minimum-evidence attack, and identifies task-relevant directions the detector cannot see. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector that flags 82.8\% of random single-channel corruptions is first-order blind on 64.7\% of task/subset pairs in an audit of one- to four-channel subsets. Task-conditioned manipulations cause more than twice as many falsely reassuring errors as generic stealthy ones, and more of them evade the alarm on four of five splits, mainly at small budgets. Used to prioritize audits on held-out subsets, the margin finds a median of four verified failures in ten checks, compared with none for random order and two for alarm-based ranking, and performs comparably to the task-gradient baseline. It also ranks vulnerable configurations of the learned GDN and TranAD detectors and of a five-source crop-yield panel.

summary: Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents. These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE). PCE distils task records and modification histories from the population into a population block, which captures recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of previously attempted modifications to guide improvements to a selected parent's harness. Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points. In our evaluation, PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by one-third on SWE-bench and closes it on Polyglot. These results suggest that treating the population as evidence--not merely as candidates for selection--provides a complementary principle for agent evolution.

summary: The landscape of software evolution is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift in the era of Large Language Models. As industrial software engineering increasingly transitions toward design-driven code generation, the bottleneck of evolution has shifted from writing code to maintaining deterministic consistency between multi-source design assets and the generated code. When a design asset changes, LLM agents currently lack a deterministic impact boundary to identify which code must be evolved, leading to two failure modes: hallucinating missing changes or breaking unrelated code. Probabilistic approaches, such as semantic retrieval or text-based diffing, fail to capture the structural ripple effects across highly interconnected design dependencies. We propose a paradigm shift from probabilistic semantic retrieval to deterministic structural constraints. We formalize the design assets as a Knowledge Graph and organize them into a content-addressed Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph. Our key insight reveals a topological isomorphism between the logical ripple effect of a design change and the content hash propagation within the DAG. By leveraging this, we transform ambiguous impact analysis into verifiable structural operations. Through a two-phase diffing process, we extract a precise causal chain that defines the exact modification boundary. This boundary enables deterministic context injection, providing the LLM agent with strictly scoped code and design updates, thereby fundamentally guaranteeing evolution safety. As a by-product, the KG serves as an agent-queryable knowledge base for natural language design retrieval. Early deployment on a large-scale industrial payment platform demonstrates that our mechanism successfully computes the exact impact boundary and generates incremental code modifications that meet the expected design changes.
title: From Ripple to Boundary: Deterministic Impact Boundaries for LLM-Based Software Evolution

summary: Benchmarks for verifiable code generation usually test a proof against one fixed implementation. We ask whether the same proof remains valid after a program refactoring that preserves behavior. We introduce RefactorProof, which derives 458 Lean-certified variants from the 185 VERINA tasks that compile in our pinned environment while holding the specification and evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. VERINA supplies reference proofs for 46 tasks, all from its basic split; the primary model-versus-reference comparisons further match on 21-25 short, non-recursive tasks. Structural refactorings expose substantial brittleness across proof sources: task-normalized structural PSR is 4.3% for the supplied references and 13.3-26.8% for the specialized provers. On the matched tasks, specialized prover proofs nevertheless have higher overall unchanged-proof survival than the supplied reference artifacts: +15.6 points for DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B, +18.8 for Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and +20.3 for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B; all three 95% CIs exclude zero. The ordering persists after excluding universally survived T1 variants, under family-balanced aggregation, and under alternative deployable valid-proof selection rules. However, unchanged-proof failure is not the same as high repair cost: predefined one-identifier edits repair 51/54 eligible reference structural failures and 58/85 eligible prover failures. RefactorProof therefore measures unchanged-proof stability under program refactoring, not the cost of maintaining a proof after it breaks.
title: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation

summary: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning uses offline pretraining to accelerate subsequent online learning. While many methods assume the offline dataset remains available throughout fine-tuning, there are many settings where this is not the case. Prior work attributes failures in this setting primarily to critic recalibration under distribution shift. We identify a complementary actor-side failure: once the offline data disappears, continued behavioral cloning (BC) no longer preserves the offline behavior distribution and instead refits the behavioral model to the agent's limited, and nonstationary, online experience. We demonstrate that stopping online behavioral fitting while preserving the pretrained expressive prior substantially improves no-retention fine-tuning across implicit flow Q-learning (IFQL), flow Q-learning (FQL), and action-chunked RL (QC) on seven OGBench domains.
